course_subtitle: Physics and Chemistry pathway, with Biology and Earth Science extension stages. Choose a topic and difficulty on the map; use the study guide for the time-limited route.

topics.title: Newtonian Mechanics Review
knowledge_points: kinematics in one and two dimensions

lesson.goal: Turn known formulas into independent model selection: first recognise the physics, then connect two ideas without being told which equations to use.
prerequisites: draw a free-body diagram when forces are involved

formula_cards.focus: Motion · choose a clock and direction
formula_cards.title: Constant acceleration and projectiles

formulas.meaning: Constant acceleration along one chosen signed axis.
symbols: u,v: initial/final velocities in m/s; a: m/s²; t: elapsed stage time in s.

formulas.meaning: Displacement uses the time elapsed in this motion stage.
symbols: s: signed displacement in m; u: initial velocity in m/s; a: m/s²; t: s.

formulas.meaning: For constant acceleration when time is not needed.
symbols: v,u: final/initial velocities in m/s; a: m/s²; s: signed displacement in m.

formulas.meaning: Launch angle θ is above horizontal; neglect drag to keep horizontal velocity constant.
symbols: u: launch speed in m/s; θ: launch angle above horizontal; x,y label horizontal and vertical components.

simple.title: One-stage check
simple.problem: A bicycle starts from rest at 2.0 m/s² for 4.0 s. Find its speed and distance.
steps: Use constant-acceleration velocity: v=0+2×4=8 m/s.
Use displacement: s=0×4+½×2×4²=16 m.
Check: average velocity is (0+8)/2=4 m/s, giving 16 m in 4 s.
simple.given: A bicycle starts from rest at 2.0 m/s² for 4.0 s.

challenge.title: Different starting times
challenge.problem: Car A passes a line at 6 m/s. Car B starts there 2 s later from rest at 4.5 m/s². Find the allowed catch-up time and position.
steps: Use t from A’s passage: x_A=6t, while x_B=2.25(t−2)² only for t≥2.
Equal positions give 2.25t²−15t+9=0, with roots t=6 and t=2/3 s.
Reject the root before B starts. At t=6 s, each position is 36 m.
challenge.answer: B catches A 6.0 s after A passes the line, at x=36 m.
challenge.given: Car A passes a line at 6 m/s. Car B starts there 2 s later from rest at 4.5 m/s².
challenge.find: Find the allowed catch-up time and position.

formula_cards.watch: An algebraic root before B starts is not physically allowed. Check the time interval before accepting a root.
background: Position and velocity are signed quantities along a chosen axis. Choose one clock, and use a new elapsed time expression for a later start or a later stage.
A projectile has one shared flight time and separate horizontal/vertical equations. Resolve its initial velocity; vertical acceleration is −g with upward positive.

formula_cards.title: Newton's laws and connected bodies

formulas.meaning: Sum external force components on one specified body or chosen system.
symbols: ΣF: resultant force component in N; m: kg; a: signed acceleration component in m/s².

formulas.meaning: Interaction partners act on different bodies; they do not cancel in one body’s force balance.
symbols: A→B means force exerted by body A on body B; both forces are in N and act on different bodies.

simple.title: One block
simple.problem: A 5 kg block has 20 N right and 5 N left acting on it. Find its acceleration.
steps: Choose right positive; the resultant is 20−5=15 N.
ΣF=ma gives a=15/5=3 m/s².
The positive sign means rightward acceleration.
simple.given: A 5 kg block has 20 N right and 5 N left acting on it.

challenge.title: Find the internal force last
challenge.problem: A 2 kg and a 3 kg block are linked on a rough floor, μₖ=0.20. A 35 N force pulls the 3 kg block. Use g=10 m/s². Find a and T.
steps: Both blocks together have 0.20×5×10=10 N floor friction.
Whole-system acceleration=(35−10)/5=5 m/s².
On the 2 kg block, T−0.20×2×10=2×5, giving T=14 N.
challenge.given: A 2 kg and a 3 kg block are linked on a rough floor, μₖ=0.20. A 35 N force pulls the 3 kg block. Use g=10 m/s².

formula_cards.watch: Tension is internal for the two-block system, but external when one block is isolated.
background: Name the object before drawing its external forces. A larger system can remove an internal string tension; isolate one body afterwards to recover it.
A light taut inextensible string over a fixed ideal pulley constrains acceleration magnitudes. Its tension is the same only when pulley rotational inertia is negligible.

formula_cards.title: Friction, normal force and slopes

formulas.meaning: Static friction adjusts up to its bound; equality is used only at impending slip.
symbols: |f_s|: friction magnitude in N; μ_s: static coefficient, no unit; N: normal contact force in N.

formulas.meaning: Magnitude of kinetic friction during sliding; direction opposes relative sliding.
symbols: f_k: sliding-friction magnitude in N; μ_k: kinetic coefficient, no unit; N: normal force in N.

formulas.meaning: Weight components along and into an incline. Other forces can also change the normal reaction.
symbols: W_parallel,W_perp: weight-component magnitudes in N; m: kg; g: m/s²; θ: incline angle to horizontal.

simple.title: Plain incline
simple.problem: A 4 kg block slides down a 30° slope with μₖ=0.25. Use g=10 m/s². Find its acceleration.
steps: The normal is 4×10cos30°=34.64 N. Sliding friction is 0.25×34.64=8.66 N uphill.
Downslope weight is 4×10sin30°=20 N.
Net downslope force is 11.34 N, so acceleration=11.34/4=2.835 m/s².
simple.given: A 4 kg block slides down a 30° slope with μₖ=0.25. Use g=10 m/s².

challenge.title: A horizontal push changes N
challenge.problem: A box of weight W moves up a 30° slope at constant speed under a horizontal push P. If μₖ=1/√3, find P/W. Find the push-to-weight ratio.
steps: The horizontal push contributes Pcos30° uphill and Psin30° into the slope, so N=Wcos30°+Psin30°.
Constant speed requires Pcos30°=Wsin30°+(1/√3)(Wcos30°+Psin30°).
challenge.given: A box of weight W moves up a 30° slope at constant speed under a horizontal push P. If μₖ=1/√3, find P/W.

formula_cards.watch: Do not write N=mg cos θ when another force pushes into or pulls away from the surface.
background: A normal reaction is perpendicular to the contact surface; friction is tangential. A tilted push or pull changes the normal force.
Static friction opposes the tendency of relative slip and can point along the motion. Kinetic friction opposes actual relative sliding. Always check which regime applies.

formula_cards.title: Work, mechanical energy and springs

formulas.meaning: Net work changes translational kinetic energy.
symbols: W_net: sum of external force work in J; ΔK: final minus initial kinetic energy in J.

formulas.meaning: Mechanical energy of a translating mass and attached ideal spring, with x from natural length.
symbols: E_mech: J; m: kg; v: m/s; g: m/s²; h: height in m; k: spring stiffness in N/m; x: spring extension/compression from natural length in m.

formulas.meaning: For constant sliding friction, d is total path length during which it acts.
symbols: W_f: friction work in J; f_k: constant sliding-friction magnitude in N; d: full travelled distance in m.

simple.title: Spring launch
simple.problem: A 0.50 kg block is launched by a 100 N/m spring compressed 0.20 m on a smooth floor. Find its speed at natural length.
steps: Initial spring energy=½×100×0.20²=2 J.
At natural length the spring has no stored energy; on the smooth floor 2=½×0.50×v².
Thus v²=8 and v=2.828 m/s.
simple.given: A 0.50 kg block is launched by a 100 N/m spring compressed 0.20 m on a smooth floor.
simple.find: Find its speed at natural length.

challenge.title: Friction acts on both sides
challenge.problem: A 2 kg block remains attached to an ideal spring, k=80 N/m, initially compressed 0.50 m on a horizontal floor with μ_k=0.25. Release it from rest; use g=10 m/s². Find the first stopping position.
steps: Initial spring energy=½×80×0.50²=10 J; sliding friction=0.25×2×10=5 N.
Let x_total be full travel. At the far turning point spring extension is x_total−0.50, so 10=5x_total+40(x_total−0.50)².
Expansion gives 40x_total²−35x_total=0. Reject zero, the starting point. The far stop is x_total=0.875 m, or 0.375 m beyond natural length.
challenge.answer: x_total=0.875 m, so it stops 0.375 m beyond natural length.
challenge.given: A 2 kg block remains attached to an ideal spring, k=80 N/m, initially compressed 0.50 m on a horizontal floor with μ_k=0.25. Release it from rest; use g=10 m/s².

formula_cards.watch: Measure friction distance along the whole path; spring compression is measured from natural length.
background: Choose initial and final states. Use spring displacement from natural length, gravity height from a consistent reference and actual distance travelled for friction work.

An ideal spring exerts restoring force −kx and stores energy ½kx². Its stored energy is non-negative on either side of natural length. Mechanical energy is conserved only when no unaccounted transfer removes or adds it.

formula_cards.focus: Rate · look for the extra factor of speed
formula_cards.title: Power and resistive forces

formulas.meaning: For force parallel to motion; average power is transferred energy divided by time.
symbols: P: W; F: force component along motion in N; v: speed in m/s.

formulas.meaning: A supplied quadratic-drag model; at steady speed drive balances drag.
symbols: F_drag: N; v: m/s; P_steady: W; coefficient c has units N·s²/m² for this drag law.

simple.title: Constant climbing speed
simple.problem: A 500 kg lift rises at 2.0 m/s at constant speed. Ignore losses and use g=10 m/s². Find required mechanical power.
steps: At steady upward speed the lifting force balances 500×10=5000 N.
Convert 10000 W to 10 kW; the lift gains 10000 J each second.
simple.given: A 500 kg lift rises at 2.0 m/s at constant speed. Ignore losses and use g=10 m/s².

challenge.title: Why double power does not double speed
challenge.problem: A car needs 8.0 kW to overcome cv² drag at 20 m/s. Find the speed at 13.5 kW.
steps: Quadratic drag needs power cv³ at steady speed.
Divide the two states: (v₂/20)³=13.5/8.0=1.6875.
Take the cube root: v₂=20×1.6875^(1/3)=23.811 m/s.
challenge.given: A car needs 8.0 kW to overcome cv² drag at 20 m/s.

formula_cards.watch: The drag force is proportional to v², but the required power is proportional to v³.
background: Power is energy transfer per second, measured in watts. At steady speed drive balances the total resistance but still does work.
A supplied resistance model may contain several terms. Infer force from P/v before fitting speed-dependent coefficients.

formula_cards.title: Momentum and impulse

formulas.meaning: Signed linear momentum along the selected axis.
symbols: p: momentum in kg·m/s; m: kg; v: signed velocity in m/s.

formulas.meaning: Impulse is signed area under a force–time graph; this does not require calculus for simple shapes.
symbols: J: impulse in N·s; Δp: momentum change in kg·m/s; F_avg: signed average force in N; Δt: s.

simple.title: A triangular pulse
simple.problem: A force rises from 0 to 12 N and returns to 0 over 0.50 s. Find the impulse.
steps: Impulse equals the area under the force–time triangle.
The base is 0.50 s and height is 12 N.
J=½×0.50×12=3.0 N·s in the force direction.
simple.given: A force rises from 0 to 12 N and returns to 0 over 0.50 s.

challenge.title: Rebound means a large Δv
challenge.problem: A 0.20 kg ball moving right at 18 m/s rebounds left at 12 m/s in 0.015 s. Find the average force on the ball.
steps: Right positive gives u=+18 m/s and v=−12 m/s.
F_avg=−6.0/0.015=−400 N, meaning 400 N left.
challenge.given: A 0.20 kg ball moving right at 18 m/s rebounds left at 12 m/s in 0.015 s.
challenge.find: Find the average force on the ball.

formula_cards.watch: On rebound, final and initial velocities have opposite signs. The change is not merely the difference of their speeds.
background: Momentum includes direction; choose signs before subtracting velocities. A rebound can produce a large change even when final speed is smaller.
Impulse is force accumulated over time. A triangular force pulse gives base×height/2; the signed impulse adds to initial momentum.

formula_cards.title: Momentum first, energy where valid

formulas.meaning: Conservation applies to a system with negligible net external impulse during the interaction.
symbols: Σ means add the signed momenta of every body in the selected system; each p is in kg·m/s.

formulas.meaning: For a one-dimensional elastic collision, relative separation speed equals relative approach speed. Momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved.
symbols: u₁,u₂: before velocities; v₁,v₂: after velocities, in m/s on one common axis.

simple.title: Sticking collision
simple.problem: A 1 kg cart at 6 m/s sticks to a stationary 2 kg cart. Find their common speed.
steps: Choose the moving cart’s direction positive; total momentum is 1×6+2×0=6 kg·m/s.
After sticking, both carts share mass 3 kg and speed V.
3V=6 gives V=2 m/s; momentum, not kinetic energy, is conserved through impact.
simple.given: A 1 kg cart at 6 m/s sticks to a stationary 2 kg cart.

challenge.title: Spring interaction between two carts
challenge.problem: A 1 kg cart at 6 m/s compresses a 200 N/m spring attached to a free 3 kg cart. Find maximum compression.
steps: At maximum compression the cart velocities match. Momentum gives 1×6=(1+3)V, so V=1.5 m/s.
Initial kinetic energy is 18 J and shared translational energy is ½×4×1.5²=4.5 J.
The spring stores 13.5 J: ½×200×x²=13.5, giving x=√0.135=0.3674 m.
challenge.given: A 1 kg cart at 6 m/s compresses a 200 N/m spring attached to a free 3 kg cart.

formula_cards.watch: Shared velocity at maximum compression does not mean the carts have stuck; the spring can re-expand.
background: First identify whether external impulse is negligible. A sticking collision conserves momentum but generally converts some kinetic energy to other forms.

An elastic collision conserves kinetic energy as well. At maximum spring compression, two interacting carts have equal instantaneous velocity; their energy difference is in the spring. Treat later swing or heating as a separate stage.

formula_cards.focus: Curved motion · write the inward equation
formula_cards.title: Circular motion and gravity

formulas.meaning: Use real inward force components; centripetal describes their resultant, not an additional force.
symbols: ΣF_in: resultant inward force in N; m: kg; v: speed in m/s; r: circle radius in m.

formulas.meaning: For a spherical planet outside its surface; r is centre-to-centre distance.
symbols: F_g: gravitational force in N; M,m: masses in kg; r: centre-to-centre separation in m; G≈6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

simple.title: Flat circular motion
simple.problem: A 2 kg object moves at 5 m/s in a circle of radius 2.5 m. Find the inward net force.
steps: Circular motion needs inward acceleration a_r=v²/r=25/2.5=10 m/s².
Multiply by mass: F_in=2×10=20 N.
This is the inward resultant of real forces, not a separate added force.
simple.given: A 2 kg object moves at 5 m/s in a circle of radius 2.5 m.

challenge.title: Minimum speed through a loop
challenge.problem: A small object moves inside a frictionless loop of radius r. Find its minimum speed at the bottom to maintain contact at the top.
steps: At the limiting top contact N=0, so mg=mv_top²/r and v_top²=gr.
The top is 2r higher: ½mv_bottom²=½mv_top²+mg×2r.
Cancel m and substitute to get v_bottom²=gr+4gr=5gr; take the positive speed.
challenge.given: A small object moves inside a frictionless loop of radius r.
challenge.find: Find its minimum speed at the bottom to maintain contact at the top.

formula_cards.watch: At a minimum-contact condition, set the contact force to zero at the critical point before using energy.
background: Uniform circular motion still accelerates inward because velocity direction changes. Resolve actual forces toward the centre.

For circular orbits gravity supplies that inward resultant; combine with speed=2πr/T for period T. G≈6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² is the universal gravitational constant. At a contact limit set the track normal or string tension to zero at the critical location.

formula_cards.title: Torque and static equilibrium

formulas.meaning: r is pivot-to-application-point distance; φ is the angle between that position vector and force.
symbols: τ: torque in N·m; r: lever-arm length in m; F: force in N; φ: angle between lever arm and force.

formulas.meaning: Static equilibrium requires both translational and rotational balance.
symbols: ΣF: signed external-force sum in N; Στ: signed external-torque sum in N·m about the chosen pivot.

simple.title: Balanced beam
simple.problem: A 30 N load hangs 2.0 m left of a pivot. Where should a 20 N load hang on the right to balance it? Find the balancing position.
steps: The left load produces anticlockwise torque 30×2=60 N·m.
The right load must produce equal clockwise torque: 20x=60.
Thus x=3 m to the right; force balance additionally determines pivot reaction.
simple.given: A 30 N load hangs 2.0 m left of a pivot. Where should a 20 N load hang on the right to balance it?

challenge.title: Slide or tip first?
challenge.problem: A block of width 1.2 m and height 2.0 m is pushed horizontally at its top. μₛ=0.50. Decide what happens first.
steps: Before tipping the floor normal is mg, so the sliding threshold is 0.50mg.
At tipping take moments about the lower edge: F×2.0=mg×0.60, so F_tip=0.30mg.
The smaller force is reached first: the block tips before it slides.
challenge.given: A block of width 1.2 m and height 2.0 m is pushed horizontally at its top. μₛ=0.50.

formula_cards.watch: A convenient pivot removes unknown reaction forces from the torque equation.
background: Torque measures the turning effect of a force about a chosen pivot. A force through the pivot has no lever arm and contributes no torque there.
For static equilibrium both net force and net torque vanish. A uniform beam’s weight acts at its centre. At tipping the floor reaction moves to the edge; compare that threshold with sliding.

formula_cards.focus: Rotation · include where energy is stored
formula_cards.title: Angular dynamics and rolling

formulas.meaning: Rigid-body angular acceleration about the specified fixed axis; I is moment of inertia.
symbols: τ: external torque in N·m; I: moment of inertia in kg·m²; α: angular acceleration in rad/s².

formulas.meaning: Rolling without slipping relates centre speed/acceleration to angular speed/acceleration magnitudes.
symbols: v,a: centre speed/acceleration in m/s and m/s²; R: rolling radius in m; ω: rad/s; α: rad/s².

formulas.meaning: Rolling energy has translational and rotational parts.
symbols: K: J; m: kg; v: centre speed in m/s; I: kg·m²; ω: angular speed in rad/s.

formulas.meaning: About a fixed axis, negligible external torque conserves angular momentum, even if internal work changes energy.
symbols: L: angular momentum in kg·m²/s; I: kg·m²; ω: rad/s, all about the same axis.

formulas.meaning: A point mass at perpendicular radius r contributes mr²; contributions add.
symbols: I_point: kg·m²; m: point mass in kg; r: perpendicular distance to the axis in m.

formulas.meaning: A uniform solid sphere about a diameter.
symbols: m: solid sphere mass in kg; R: physical radius in m; I: moment of inertia in kg·m² about a diameter.

formulas.meaning: A uniform solid cylinder/disc about its symmetry axis.
symbols: m: cylinder/disc mass in kg; R: radius in m; I: kg·m² about its central symmetry axis.

simple.title: Rolling energy
simple.problem: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping at 4 m/s. Its moment of inertia is I=½mR² about its central axis. Express its total kinetic energy in terms of its mass m, measured in kg.
steps: No slip gives ω=v/R.
K=½mv²+½(½mR²)(v²/R²)=¾mv².
At v=4 m/s this is ¾m×16=12m J, with m in kg.
simple.given: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping at 4 m/s. Its moment of inertia is I=½mR² about its central axis.
simple.find: Express its total kinetic energy in terms of its mass m, measured in kg.

challenge.title: Rolling down an incline
challenge.problem: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping through a vertical drop h. Find its speed at the bottom.
steps: No-loss energy conservation gives mgh=½mv²+½Iω².
Use I=½mR² and ω=v/R, giving mgh=¾mv².
Cancel m and solve: v²=4gh/3, so v=√(4gh/3).
challenge.given: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping through a vertical drop h.
challenge.find: Find its speed at the bottom.

formula_cards.watch: A rolling object usually has less translational speed than a sliding point mass after the same vertical drop.
background: Moment of inertia I measures resistance to angular acceleration and depends on how mass is distributed about the selected axis. Angular speed ω is in rad/s and angular acceleration α in rad/s².
For rolling without slipping, centre motion and spin are linked. Static friction can supply the torque; for ideal rolling on a fixed surface its contact point does not slide.
For an isolated spinning system, no external torque conserves L=Iω. Moving masses inward decreases I and raises ω; the required internal work can increase rotational kinetic energy.

model_routine.title: Use the smallest hint first
steps: Name the system and draw only the forces acting on it.
Ask what changes: motion, energy, momentum, or rotation?
Write one governing equation before inserting numbers.
If the situation changes, split it into stages and change models deliberately.
Check units, signs, physical limits and whether every constraint is satisfied.

learning_map.big_idea: Choose the object or system first. Motion describes what changes; forces explain its acceleration; energy and momentum provide alternative accounts when their conditions hold.

basics.title: Describe motion before explaining it
basics.story: Velocity includes direction. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so turning at constant speed still requires acceleration. A graph of velocity against time gives acceleration by its slope and displacement by its signed area.
basics.why: The motion description tells you which force component or energy change must be explained. Constant-acceleration equations apply only while acceleration stays constant.
basics.symbols: u and v: initial/final signed velocity (m/s); a: acceleration (m/s²); t: elapsed time (s); s: displacement (m).

basics.title: A net force changes one object’s velocity
basics.story: Draw only the forces acting on your chosen object. Add their components in the same direction before applying Newton’s second law. An interaction pair acts on different objects.
basics.why: Balanced forces mean zero acceleration; the object may still move at a constant velocity. A centripetal force is the inward resultant of real forces.
basics.symbols: ΣF: vector sum of forces (N); m: mass (kg); a: acceleration (m/s²).

basics.title: Work changes kinetic energy
basics.story: Work transfers energy when a force acts through a displacement. Net work changes kinetic energy; gravity, springs and friction may transfer energy into different stores.
basics.why: For a fixed force acting from rest, doubling the final speed requires four times the accelerating distance; the work and kinetic energy are four times as large.
basics.symbols: W_net: net work (J); Δ means final minus initial; K: kinetic energy (J); K=½mv². Choose the system before using energy conservation.

basics.title: Momentum accounts for interactions over time
basics.story: Momentum is mass times velocity. Impulse is the net force accumulated over time and equals the change of momentum.
basics.why: For a chosen system, internal interaction impulses cancel; total momentum is conserved only when the external impulse is zero or negligible. Kinetic energy need not be conserved in a collision.
basics.symbols: p: momentum (kg m/s); J: impulse (N s); F_avg: time-averaged net force (N); Δt: time interval (s).

routes.title: Review the basic descriptions
routes.cue: A graph, a slope, a force diagram or a single energy change.
routes.connection: Connect motion to its cause before combining systems.

routes.title: Combine accounts and constraints
routes.cue: Bodies touch, collide, turn, or remain balanced.
routes.connection: Apply friction bounds, momentum, inward force or torque only after stating the system and constraints.

routes.title: Extend to rotation
routes.cue: A pulley has inertia, an object rolls, or translation and rotation share energy.
routes.connection: Start from the earlier force/energy account, then add angular motion and the no-slip condition when it is justified.

learning_map.checkpoint: Can you name the system and explain why you chose force, energy or momentum before substituting? Mechanics practice starts at Core.

medium.context: A rescue package is launched at 20.0 m/s and 30° above horizontal from a platform 15.0 m above level ground. Use g = 10 m/s² and neglect air resistance.
medium.prompt: How far horizontally from the launch point does the package land?
medium.hint: Find the flight time from vertical motion, then use horizontal velocity.
medium.feedback_correct: Correct. t=3 s gives ground height zero and horizontal range 51.96 m.
medium.feedback_incorrect: The package starts 15 m above ground; a level-ground flight-time shortcut does not apply.
medium.explanation: Projectile components share one landing time with independent axis equations. Vertical motion gives 0=15+(20sin30°)t−5t², whose positive root is t=3.00 s. Therefore x=(20cos30°)(3.00)=52.0 m.
medium.given: A rescue package is launched at 20.0 m/s and 30° above horizontal from a platform 15.0 m above level ground. Use g = 10 m/s² and neglect air resistance.
medium.find: How far horizontally from the launch point does the package land?

worked_solution.tested_idea: Projectile components share one landing time with independent axis equations
worked_solution.model: Projectile components share one landing time with independent axis equations.

formulas.meaning: Launch angle θ is above horizontal; neglect drag to keep horizontal velocity constant.
Displacement uses the time elapsed in this motion stage.

steps: Projectile components share one landing time with independent axis equations.
Vertical motion gives 0=15+(20sin30°)t−5t², whose positive root is t=3.00 s.
Therefore x=(20cos30°)(3.00)=52.0 m.
worked_solution.check: t=3 s gives ground height zero and horizontal range 51.96 m.

easy.prompt: Explain why the pressure first rises to 190 kPa and then falls to 160 kPa even though the piston does not move during the waiting period.
easy.hint: Separate the rapid compression from the later constant-volume cooling.
easy.feedback_correct: Good. You connected the transient pressure to warming, cooling and changing wall collisions.
easy.feedback_partial: You have part of the chain. Include why rapid compression warms the gas and why cooling lowers pressure at fixed volume.
easy.feedback_incorrect: Explain the energy and particle changes during both stages.
easy.explanation: Rapid work on the gas raises its internal energy and temperature, so faster particles produce a high pressure. While the piston is fixed, thermal energy passes to the surroundings; the particles slow and transfer momentum to the walls less rapidly, so pressure falls.
easy.context: A sealed syringe is compressed rapidly and clamped. A sensor reads 190 kPa immediately and 160 kPa after one minute.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Rapid compression followed by constant-volume cooling
worked_solution.model: Mechanical work first changes the gas temperature; later thermal transfer changes pressure while volume remains fixed.
steps: Rapid compression does work on the gas, increasing internal energy and temperature.
Faster particles collide with the walls more often and transfer more momentum, producing the 190 kPa peak.
With the piston clamped, V and n stay fixed while energy leaves to the surroundings.
As the gas cools, collision rate and momentum transfer fall, so pressure settles at 160 kPa.
worked_solution.final_answer: The peak is a hot transient; 160 kPa is the cooler settled pressure.
worked_solution.check: The pressure can change at fixed volume because P/T remains constant for a fixed amount of ideal gas.
worked_solution.common_error: Saying the pressure falls because the volume increases; the problem states that the piston is fixed.

hard.explanation: The outer enclosure is insulated and rigid. There is no heat input or external volume work, so gas energy is conserved; no gas escapes, so total amount is also conserved. application_brief.title: Internal energy and molar heat capacity
application_brief.background: Internal energy U is energy stored microscopically, measured in joules. For an ideal gas with constant molar heat capacity at fixed volume C_V, a temperature change gives ΔU=nC_VΔT. Here n is amount in mol, C_V is energy per mole per kelvin in J/(mol K), and ΔT is in K. Total heat capacity is nC_V in J/K; mass-specific c is in J/(kg K). Different ideal gases may have different C_V. For a monatomic ideal gas C_V=3R/2; choose one common energy reference. In a rigid insulated mixing system there is no external work or heat, so total internal energy is conserved.

application_brief.title: Gas thermometers and phase change
application_brief.background: A gas thermometer infers temperature from gas pressure in a sealed bulb. At sufficiently low temperature a real gas can form liquid: condensation transfers particles out of the gas phase. In liquid–vapour equilibrium, evaporation and condensation balance on average. For a pure substance at a fixed temperature with both phases present, the equilibrium vapour pressure is fixed even while the amounts in the phases change.

formula_cards.watch: Temperature measures average random kinetic energy. It is not the speed of every particle, and particles do not all move at one speed.
background: Gas pressure is a macroscopic effect produced by microscopic collisions. Each particle changes momentum when it rebounds from a wall; the wall experiences an equal and opposite force.
Pressure tells us how concentrated that force is over an area. Temperature tells us about the average random kinetic energy of the particles, not the speed of every individual particle.

The ideal-gas model treats particles as very small compared with their spacing and neglects attractions between collisions. It is a useful approximation for dilute gas away from condensation. Heating or compression can eventually move a real gas outside this range.

formula_cards.watch: State the conditions before naming a law. Boyle’s law requires constant temperature; Charles’s law requires constant pressure; the pressure–temperature law requires constant volume.
background: For the same sealed sample of ideal gas, PV/T has the same value in every equilibrium state. The combined gas law compares two such states.
Boyle’s, Charles’s and the pressure–temperature law are special cases. Each name tells you which quantity is held constant. A named law cannot be used unless its conditions are satisfied.

In a Boyle apparatus, move the syringe piston in steps and wait for the pressure and temperature to settle before recording each point. The trapped gas includes the syringe barrel, nozzle, connecting tube and sensor port.
Boyle’s law gives a curved pressure-versus-volume graph. Plotting absolute pressure against reciprocal total volume, 1/V, gives a straight-line test over the range where the model applies.

A frictionless piston is a movable boundary. In a settled state the gas force PA balances atmospheric force and the load. For a fixed cross-sectional area A, moving the piston by distance Δx changes the gas volume by AΔx. Draw the forces before deciding whether pressure is constant.

Linearisation means choosing new graph axes so a curved relationship becomes a straight line. From PV=K, division by V gives P=K(1/V): the reciprocal 1/V is the horizontal variable and the gradient is K=nRT. This gradient has pressure × volume units. A fitted line supports the model only over the measured range; repeat readings and inspect departures from the line.

Measured value minus the prediction at the same input. A systematic pattern can reveal a model or calibration problem.
A change, normally final minus initial. For example ΔV is a volume change.

formula_cards.watch: Use R with amount n in moles. Use k<sub>B</sub> with particle number N.
background: The ideal-gas equation can describe gas amount in moles or as an actual number of particles. These are two ways of counting the same gas.

In PV=Nk<sub>B</sub>T, N/V measures how many particles share each unit of volume and k<sub>B</sub>T is an energy scale per particle. More particles at the same V and T give more wall impacts. For a fixed sample, N is unchanged, so dividing by T gives constant PV/T. With n moles, N=nN<sub>A</sub>; replacing N by nN<sub>A</sub> gives R=N<sub>A</sub>k<sub>B</sub> and PV=nRT.

Use Pa and m³ with R=8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹: 1 Pa m³=1 J. One litre is 10⁻³ m³; 1 cm³ is 10⁻⁶ m³. In a ratio, matching volume units cancel; in an absolute particle-count calculation, units must match the constant.

Mass and amount are different. Molar mass M is the mass of one mole: n=m/M, using the same mass unit for m and M. Density ρ=m/V is mass per volume. A sealed nonreacting sample keeps its mass and amount even when its volume and density change. For connected regions, add their amounts; use each region’s own temperature.

lesson.introduction_heading: The physical story before the formulas

introduction.title: What is a gas?
introduction.body: A gas contains a very large number of particles moving randomly. The particles travel between collisions, strike the container walls and exert pressure. A gas expands to fill the space available to it.

introduction.title: What describes one gas state?
introduction.body: A state is one settled condition of the gas. We describe it with absolute pressure P, volume V, absolute temperature T and the amount of gas. State 1 means before a change; State 2 means after it.

introduction.title: What changes pressure?
introduction.body: Pressure rises when wall collisions transfer momentum more often or more strongly. This can happen when the gas is compressed, heated or supplied with more particles.

introduction.title: What does a gas law mean?
introduction.body: A gas law is an experimentally tested relationship that works only under stated conditions. Before using one, identify what stays constant and whether the same amount of gas remains trapped.

lesson.symbol_heading: Names, meanings and SI units used in this lesson

items.name: Pressure
items.meaning: Force per unit area exerted by the gas. Gas laws use absolute pressure measured from vacuum.

items.name: Volume
items.meaning: The space occupied by the gas. Use one consistent volume unit within a ratio.
items.unit: m³ in SI; L, mL and cm³ are also common

items.name: Absolute temperature
items.meaning: Temperature measured from absolute zero. Gas-law ratios must use kelvin.

items.name: State subscripts
items.meaning: Subscript 1 labels the initial state and subscript 2 labels the final state.

items.name: Amount of gas
items.meaning: The amount of substance measured in moles. One mole contains exactly 6.02214076×10²³ specified particles.

items.name: Universal gas constant
items.meaning: The constant used when gas amount is measured in moles: R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

items.name: Number of particles
items.meaning: The actual count of atoms or molecules in the gas. It is a number, not a force.

items.name: Boltzmann constant
items.meaning: The constant used for individual particles: k<sub>B</sub> = 1.380649×10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

items.name: Celsius temperature
items.meaning: Temperature stated on the Celsius scale before conversion to kelvin.

items.name: Pressure labels
items.meaning: abs means absolute, gauge means above atmospheric pressure, and atm means atmospheric pressure.

items.name: Proportional to
items.meaning: One quantity changes by the same factor as another while the stated conditions remain fixed.

learning_map.big_idea: Gas pressure, volume and temperature describe the same moving particles. First decide what the container allows to change and whether the number of particles stays fixed.

basics.title: Collisions produce pressure
basics.story: A gas contains many particles moving randomly. When they collide with a wall, their momentum changes and they exert forces on it. Pressure measures normal force per unit area.
basics.why: Heating the same ideal gas increases average random kinetic energy. If the volume is fixed, collisions transfer more momentum to the walls; the pressure rises.
basics.symbols: P: pressure (Pa=N/m²); F: normal force (N); A: area (m²).

basics.title: Use absolute temperature and pressure
basics.story: Kelvin temperature is measured from absolute zero. Absolute pressure is measured from a vacuum; gauge pressure is the difference from the surrounding atmospheric pressure.
basics.why: Gas-law ratios use kelvin and absolute pressure. A rise of 1°C is a rise of 1 K, but 20°C is not twice the absolute temperature of 10°C.
basics.symbols: T_K: temperature (K); θ_C: Celsius temperature (°C); P_abs=P_gauge+P_atm, with all pressures in the same unit.

basics.title: One state equation connects the quantities
basics.story: For an ideal gas, pressure times volume depends on temperature and the amount of gas. A sealed, non-reacting sample keeps its amount fixed; leaking or dissociation can change that amount.
basics.why: At fixed amount, PV/T stays constant. Named gas laws are choices about which variable is held fixed, not unrelated rules to memorise.
basics.symbols: P: absolute pressure (Pa); V: volume (m³); n: amount (mol); T: kelvin temperature (K). One mole contains exactly 6.02214076×10²³ specified entities. R≈8.314 J/(mol K) is the universal gas constant.

formula.meaning: Use SI units together: Pa m³ = J.

basics.title: A flexible boundary responds to outside pressure
basics.story: A bubble or freely moving piston changes volume until mechanical forces balance. In a resting liquid, pressure increases with depth because the liquid above has weight.
basics.why: The gas state equation describes the gas; the surrounding liquid or piston supplies an additional pressure condition. For a large bubble at rest, neglecting surface tension, inside and outside pressures match.
basics.symbols: ρ: liquid density (kg/m³); g: gravitational acceleration (m/s²); h: depth (m); surface pressure is P_atm when exposed to the atmosphere.

routes.title: Compare a sealed sample
routes.cue: The same non-reacting gas is heated, compressed or moved to a different depth.
routes.connection: Begin with PV/T and identify the fixed variable; read the named laws and basic pressure account here.

routes.title: Count how much gas is present
routes.cue: The question gives a mass, molar mass or number of particles.
routes.connection: Connect the macroscopic state to amount; keep molar amount n and particle count N separate.

routes.title: Use an unfamiliar apparatus
routes.cue: A tube has an unmarked volume, a sensor offset, a leaking boundary or a reaction.
routes.connection: Use the same state equation plus the apparatus conditions supplied at first use. Derive the measurement relation rather than collecting a separate formula for every apparatus.

learning_map.checkpoint: Can you say what stays fixed, whether gas amount changes, and why your pressure and temperature are absolute?

formula_cards.focus: THERMAL QUANTITIES · define the system first
formula_cards.title: Temperature, internal energy and heat transfer

formulas.meaning: Radiation uses kelvin absolute temperature. Heating calculations use temperature changes, whose numerical size is the same in °C and K.
symbols: T<sub>K</sub> — kelvin temperature; θ<sub>C</sub> — Celsius temperature.
Δ means final minus initial when describing a change.

formulas.meaning: Energy entering minus energy leaving changes stored internal energy when bulk motion, gravitational changes and other stores are negligible. Include electrical work as an input when present.
symbols: ΔU — internal-energy change in J.
E<sub>in</sub> and E<sub>out</sub> — all included energy transfers in J.

steps: draw the system boundary
list energy entering
list energy stored
list energy leaving

simple.title: Same temperature, different internal energy
simple.problem: Water samples of 0.10 kg and 0.50 kg are both at 40 °C and in the same liquid phase. Use the same internal-energy reference. Compare their temperature and total internal energy.
steps: Their equal temperatures mean no net heat would flow between them on contact.
The samples have the same material and phase but the larger contains five times the water mass.
With the same energy reference, its internal energy is five times as large; temperature alone does not measure a sample’s total energy.
simple.answer: The 0.50 kg sample has more internal energy.
simple.given: Water samples of 0.10 kg and 0.50 kg are both at 40 °C and in the same liquid phase. Use the same internal-energy reference.
simple.find: Compare their temperature and total internal energy.

challenge.title: What else is being heated?
challenge.problem: An electrical heater and thermometer are embedded in a metal block. All three warm, and some energy leaves to the room. Identify the energy terms when the chosen system is the block plus heater and thermometer.
steps: Electrical work brings energy through the system boundary.
Stored internal energy increases in the block, heater and thermometer.
Subtract energy escaping to the room to obtain the increase in total stored energy.
challenge.answer: The block alone does not receive all of the electrical input energy.
challenge.given: An electrical heater and thermometer are embedded in a metal block. All three warm, and some energy leaves to the room.
challenge.find: Identify the energy terms when the chosen system is the block plus heater and thermometer.

formula_cards.watch: Heat is energy crossing a boundary because of a temperature difference. A body stores internal energy; it does not store ‘heat’ as a separate substance.
background: Choose a fixed reference when comparing stored energy. For the same substance in the same phase at the same temperature, a larger mass has a larger internal energy relative to that reference. Equal temperature alone does not establish equal total stored energy.

Within one phase, warming usually increases microscopic motion. A phase change can also change particle arrangement and microscopic potential energy. Temperature proportional to mean translational kinetic energy is a classical ideal-gas result; it is not a general equation for every solid and liquid.

terms.definition: Bodies in thermal contact have reached the same temperature, with no net heat transfer between them.
The imaginary line deciding which objects and energy stores belong in your account.
The measured state stays constant with time. Energy may still flow in and out at equal rates.

figures.title: Draw the energy account
figures.alt: Electrical input enters a sample and its apparatus. Energy can increase stored internal energy or leave to the room.
figures.caption: The boundary decides which apparatus energy stores are included. Equal input and output powers give steady state.

formula_cards.focus: ONE PHASE · heating, power and efficiency
formula_cards.title: Sensible heating and net power

formulas.meaning: Within one phase, thermal energy absorbed raises temperature; the signed relation gives a negative Q for cooling. Assume constant c and negligible mechanical work.
symbols: m — kg; c — J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; ΔT — K; Q — J.

formulas.meaning: Heat capacity refers to the whole selected object, including any parts in a calibrated apparatus.
symbols: C — J K⁻¹; c — J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

formulas.meaning: Constant power multiplied by elapsed time gives input energy.
symbols: P — W; t — s; E — J.

formulas.meaning: Choose the useful output named in the question; a percentage is 100 times this fraction.
symbols: η — efficiency between 0 and 1 for the stated passive energy account.

formulas.meaning: Incoming power first replaces outgoing losses; the difference changes stored thermal energy.
symbols: dT/dt — signed tangent slope in K s⁻¹; C — J K⁻¹.
P<sub>in</sub> and P<sub>out</sub> — non-negative pathway magnitudes in W.

simple.title: Warm a water sample
simple.problem: Warm 0.50 kg of water from 20 °C to 50 °C. Use c=4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; no phase change occurs. Find the energy absorbed by the water.
steps: The temperature change is 50−20=30 °C, equal to a 30 K interval.
Divide by 1000 to obtain Q=63 kJ.
simple.given: Warm 0.50 kg of water from 20 °C to 50 °C. Use c=4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; no phase change occurs.
simple.find: Find the energy absorbed by the water.

challenge.title: Measure average heat loss
challenge.problem: A 1.8 kW heater warms 1.20 kg of water by 70 K in 220 s. Use c=4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and neglect apparatus heat capacity. Find the average power transferred to the room.
steps: Electrical input is 1800×220=396000 J; water storage is 1.20×4200×70=352800 J.
The missing 43200 J is the loss to the room under the stated negligible-apparatus assumption.
Average loss power=43200/220=196 W.
challenge.given: A 1.8 kW heater warms 1.20 kg of water by 70 K in 220 s. Use c=4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and neglect apparatus heat capacity.
challenge.find: Find the average power transferred to the room.

formula_cards.watch: Use kilograms with J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and seconds with watts. A Celsius temperature difference equals the same kelvin difference. Use net power when losses matter.
background: Specific heat capacity c describes one kilogram of a material. The whole object’s heat capacity C includes its mass: doubling the mass doubles the energy required for the same temperature change. A cup or device with a supplied C needs Q=CΔT; do not multiply that C by mass again.

One watt means one joule transferred per second. For a short interval with no phase change, net energy is CΔT. Dividing by the interval gives net power=C×temperature slope. A graph tangent gives the slope at a chosen instant.

formula_cards.focus: PHASE CHANGE · split the thermal journey
formula_cards.title: Latent heat and heating curves

formulas.meaning: Use the mass actually changing phase. This is an energy magnitude; assign the direction in the surrounding energy account.
symbols: L<sub>f</sub> — fusion latent heat; L<sub>v</sub> — vaporisation latent heat, in J kg⁻¹.
m — kg; Q — J. L here is not a length.

formulas.meaning: Split the journey at every transition and add the sensible and latent stages with their directions.
symbols: Σ means sum all required stages.
Use c for the phase present during each temperature-changing stage.

steps: higher-energy molecules escape
latent energy leaves the liquid
the remaining liquid cools
airflow removes vapour and sustains evaporation

simple.title: Melt ice at 0 °C
simple.problem: A 0.20 kg ice sample begins at 0 °C. Use L<sub>f</sub>=334 kJ kg⁻¹ at atmospheric pressure. Find the energy to melt it completely to water at 0 °C.
steps: The requested journey is a phase change at the transition temperature.
Use the latent energy magnitude Q=mL<sub>f</sub>=0.20×334=66.8 kJ.
The water finishes at 0 °C; no extra sensible-heating stage is requested.
simple.given: A 0.20 kg ice sample begins at 0 °C. Use L<sub>f</sub>=334 kJ kg⁻¹ at atmospheric pressure.
simple.find: Find the energy to melt it completely to water at 0 °C.

challenge.title: Ice to steam
challenge.problem: At atmospheric pressure, convert 0.010 kg ice at −10 °C to steam at 100 °C. Use c<sub>ice</sub>=2.1 and c<sub>water</sub>=4.2 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L<sub>f</sub>=334 and L<sub>v</sub>=2260 kJ kg⁻¹. Neglect losses. Find the total required energy.
steps: Warm the liquid: 0.010×4.2×100=4.200 kJ; vaporise it: 0.010×2260=22.600 kJ.
Add all four positive inputs: E_total=30.350 kJ.
challenge.answer: 30.35 kJ; most is required for vaporisation.
challenge.given: At atmospheric pressure, convert 0.010 kg ice at −10 °C to steam at 100 °C. Use c<sub>ice</sub>=2.1 and c<sub>water</sub>=4.2 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L<sub>f</sub>=334 and L<sub>v</sub>=2260 kJ kg⁻¹. Neglect losses.

formula_cards.watch: Do not apply mcΔT across a phase change. Use the net heating power for a real plateau when heat loss is significant.
background: Melting and freezing are opposite changes between solid and liquid. Vaporisation and condensation are opposite changes between liquid and gas. At a pure substance’s transition temperature and fixed pressure, a phase change can absorb or release energy without changing temperature.

Specific latent heat is a positive magnitude. Melting and vaporisation absorb mL; freezing and condensation release the same magnitude under the stated reversible school model. Boiling occurs throughout a liquid at its boiling temperature; evaporation can occur at a surface below that temperature and remove energy from the remaining liquid.

terms.definition: A horizontal interval in a temperature–time graph. For the stated pure-sample phase-change model, energy changes phase fractions while temperature remains at the transition value.

formula_cards.focus: CALORIMETRY · conserve energy and test the final state
formula_cards.title: Thermal equilibrium with possible phase change

formulas.meaning: For internal exchanges in an insulated mixture with no external work, the signed heat changes of all included parts sum to zero.
symbols: Q<sub>i</sub> — positive for an absorbing part, negative for a releasing part, in J.
The subscript i labels each included object or stage.

formulas.meaning: Equivalently, add all positive released-energy magnitudes and set their total equal to all positive absorbed-energy magnitudes.
symbols: Include the cup with Q<sub>cup</sub>=C<sub>cup</sub>ΔT when its heat capacity matters.
Use either signed Q or positive magnitudes consistently.

logic.trigger: When ice or steam is present
steps: choose the transition temperature
find energy available to reach it
compare with latent energy required
identify the phases that remain
then solve for final temperature

simple.title: Equal water samples
simple.problem: Equal masses of water at 80 °C and 20 °C mix in an insulated cup of negligible heat capacity. Assume constant water c and no phase change. Find the final equilibrium temperature.
steps: Set positive released energy mc(80−T) equal to absorbed energy mc(T−20).
The common mc cancels, giving 80−T=T−20.
Hence 2T=100 and T=50 °C, between the initial temperatures.
simple.given: Equal masses of water at 80 °C and 20 °C mix in an insulated cup of negligible heat capacity. Assume constant water c and no phase change.

challenge.title: Ice added to warm water
challenge.problem: Add 0.050 kg ice at −10 °C to 0.30 kg water at 40 °C in an insulated negligible-capacity cup. Use c<sub>ice</sub>=2.1, c<sub>water</sub>=4.2 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and L<sub>f</sub>=334 kJ kg⁻¹. Determine the final phase and temperature.
steps: Cooling the initial liquid to 0 °C releases 0.30×4.2×40=50.4 kJ.
Warming and melting the ice needs 0.050×2.1×10+0.050×334=17.75 kJ, so all the ice can melt.
The remaining 32.65 kJ warms the total 0.35 kg water: T=32.65/(0.35×4.2)=22.2 °C.
challenge.given: Add 0.050 kg ice at −10 °C to 0.30 kg water at 40 °C in an insulated negligible-capacity cup. Use c<sub>ice</sub>=2.1, c<sub>water</sub>=4.2 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and L<sub>f</sub>=334 kJ kg⁻¹.
challenge.find: Determine the final phase and temperature.

formula_cards.watch: A calculated temperature is valid only if the assumed phases are possible. Check complete melting or condensation before solving above or below a transition temperature.
background: Calorimetry uses measured temperature and phase changes to determine energy transfers. A calorimeter is the container and measuring apparatus included in that energy account. Insulation reduces exchange with the room; it does not remove energy transferred between the materials inside.

Before solving for a final temperature, test a possible transition state. With ice and water near atmospheric pressure, compare energy released on cooling to 0 °C against energy needed to warm and melt the ice. If melting is incomplete, equilibrium can contain both phases at 0 °C. A sufficiently cold added object can instead freeze some liquid.

formula_cards.focus: CONDUCTION AND CONVECTION · follow every pathway
formula_cards.title: Thermal resistance networks and fluid circulation

formulas.meaning: Use for a uniform steady layer with constant conductivity and negligible edge loss. Heat flows from hot to cold; ΔT is the positive boundary difference for the displayed magnitude.
symbols: k<sub>cond</sub> — W m⁻¹ K⁻¹; A — m²; ℓ — m.
P — W; R — K W⁻¹.

formulas.meaning: Thermal resistance packages the material and geometry into one path property.
symbols: Greater thickness increases R; greater conductivity or area decreases R.

formulas.meaning: Add series temperature drops; add parallel powers at the common temperature difference.
symbols: R<sub>i</sub> — each positive path resistance in K W⁻¹.
Σ means sum over the layers or branches.

steps: metal: lattice vibration and mobile electrons
fluid heating: density falls
buoyancy drives circulation
small cells or vacuum suppress convection

simple.title: Two layers in series
simple.problem: Two steady thermal layers connect 90 °C and 20 °C, with R₁=1.5 K/W next to the hot boundary and R₂=3.5 K/W next to the cold boundary. Ignore other paths. Find the interface temperature.
steps: The layers are in series: R_total=1.5+3.5=5.0 K/W.
The common heat rate is (90−20)/5.0=14 W.
The first layer’s temperature drop is 14×1.5=21 K, so the interface is 90−21=69 °C.
simple.given: Two steady thermal layers connect 90 °C and 20 °C, with R₁=1.5 K/W next to the hot boundary and R₂=3.5 K/W next to the cold boundary. Ignore other paths.

challenge.title: A narrow thermal bridge
challenge.problem: Insulation of R=8.0 K/W and a fastener of R=0.75 K/W form parallel paths between boundaries 30 K apart. Assume steady state. Find the percentage of heat transfer through the fastener.
steps: Each branch experiences 30 K: insulation carries 30/8.0=3.75 W and fastener carries 30/0.75=40.0 W.
The total power is 3.75+40.0=43.75 W.
Fastener percentage=100×40.0/43.75=91.4%; a narrow low-resistance path can dominate.
challenge.answer: The fastener carries 91.4% of the total heat transfer.
challenge.given: Insulation of R=8.0 K/W and a fastener of R=0.75 K/W form parallel paths between boundaries 30 K apart. Assume steady state.
challenge.find: Find the percentage of heat transfer through the fastener.

formula_cards.watch: A thin solid support can dominate a well-insulated structure. A vacuum suppresses convection and gas conduction, while the neck and supports remain solid conduction paths.
background: Conduction transfers energy through interactions within matter; a metal also has mobile electrons that transport energy. A larger temperature difference increases the driving gradient, a larger area provides more parallel paths, and greater thickness lengthens the path. The material’s thermal conductivity sets its response.

Series layers share one steady heat rate because the intermediate boundary is not storing energy. Parallel paths connect the same two boundary temperatures and carry separate heat flows that add. A thermal bridge is an extra comparatively easy path, such as a metal fastener through insulation.

Convection carries energy with moving liquid or gas. In natural convection, warming commonly makes a fluid expand and reduce its density; buoyancy can then set up circulation in gravity. Fans and pumps drive forced convection. A vacuum suppresses gas convection and gas conduction; solid supports and radiation can still transfer energy.

figures.title: Follow the heat paths
figures.alt: A serial two-layer wall has one heat path and an interface. Parallel insulation and bridge paths connect the same hot and cold boundaries.
figures.caption: At steady state: series paths carry the same power; parallel branches share the boundary temperature difference.

formula_cards.title: Emissivity and radiative equilibrium

formulas.meaning: This is outgoing emission only; a surrounding radiation field can return energy to the surface.
symbols: ε — no unit; σ=5.67×10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
A — emitting area in m²; T — surface absolute temperature in K.

formulas.meaning: Use this net-exchange form under the stated large-enclosure grey-surface assumptions. It is positive for loss when T>T<sub>s</sub>.
symbols: T<sub>s</sub> — effective surroundings temperature in K.
P<sub>net</sub> — net outgoing radiation in W.

formulas.meaning: At steady temperature with radiation as the only exchange, absorbed and emitted powers balance. Other heat paths must be included when present.
symbols: P<sub>abs</sub> and P<sub>emit</sub> — absorbed and emitted powers in W.

simple.title: Surface finish
simple.problem: Compare an ordinary dull black laboratory coating with polished metal at the same temperature and emitting area. Use their usual high and low thermal emissivities, respectively. Which emits more thermal radiation?
steps: Outgoing power is εσAT⁴.
With the same A and T, the only changing factor is ε.
The higher-emissivity dull black coating emits more thermal radiation.
simple.answer: The dull black surface is the stronger thermal-radiation emitter.
simple.given: Compare an ordinary dull black laboratory coating with polished metal at the same temperature and emitting area. Use their usual high and low thermal emissivities, respectively.

challenge.title: A spacecraft coating degrades
challenge.problem: A spacecraft’s absorbed input and emitting area remain fixed. Emissivity falls from 0.80 to 0.40. Ignore surrounding radiation and other heat paths. Find the ratio of new to old steady absolute temperature.
steps: At each steady state absorbed power equals εσAT⁴.
Fixed input and area give 0.80T_old⁴=0.40T_new⁴.
Take the positive fourth root: T_new/T_old=2^(1/4)=1.189. This is a kelvin temperature ratio.
challenge.answer: The new equilibrium temperature is 1.189 times the old value.
challenge.given: A spacecraft’s absorbed input and emitting area remain fixed. Emissivity falls from 0.80 to 0.40. Ignore surrounding radiation and other heat paths.
challenge.find: Find the ratio of new to old steady absolute temperature.

formula_cards.watch: Use kelvin for every fourth power. Treat absorbed short-wave input and emitted thermal radiation using the separately stated surface properties. Radiation can cross a vacuum.
background: All surfaces emit electromagnetic radiation because of their temperature. Emissivity ε compares thermal emission with an ideal black body at the same temperature and area. A dull black laboratory coating usually has high thermal emissivity; polished metal usually has low thermal emissivity. Visible colour alone does not determine infrared behaviour.

For a small grey surface in a large uniform surrounding enclosure, the same effective emissivity can be used for outgoing and absorbed thermal radiation in the supplied model. Net loss is emitted power minus incoming absorbed radiation. Kelvin is essential before taking a fourth power.

Incoming sunlight or a lamp can have a different spectrum from the emitted infrared. Use the separately stated reflected fraction to find absorbed input. Incident flux is incoming power per area in W/m²; multiplying flux by the area that intercepts it gives incident power. Identify the intercepting area and emitting area separately.

formula_cards.focus: LOSSES AND EVIDENCE · read the whole curve
formula_cards.title: Steady state, cooling and thermal experiments

formulas.meaning: A simple supplied model for a device warmer than its room; its coefficient must be tested rather than assumed constant over every temperature.
symbols: k<sub>loss</sub> — W K⁻¹; T−T<sub>room</sub> — K or a Celsius difference.

formulas.meaning: At steady temperature the storage term is zero, so input and total loss powers match.
symbols: Energy flow can remain nonzero at steady state.

formulas.meaning: For a uniform-temperature solid specimen and embedded apparatus with no phase change, divide electrical input between specimen storage, apparatus storage and energy leaving to the room.
symbols: V — volts; I — amperes; t — seconds.
C<sub>app</sub> — apparatus heat capacity in J K⁻¹; E<sub>loss</sub> — J.

logic.trigger: Read a heating or cooling graph
steps: slope gives net heating rate
plateau duration gives latent energy
flattening shows increasing loss
cooling data estimates loss power
if P=aV², write E=(aV²−H)t
use two trials to eliminate unknowns
check the threshold aV²=H
track T−T<sub>room</sub>
apply each halving to the excess
do not halve Celsius temperature itself

simple.title: A linear loss model
simple.problem: A device has a constant 120 W heater in a room at 20 °C. Its supplied loss model is P_loss=k<sub>loss</sub>(T−20), with k<sub>loss</sub>=3.0 W/K. Find the predicted steady device temperature.
steps: At steady temperature the stored-energy change is zero.
Set input equal to loss: 120=3.0(T−20).
The temperature excess is 40 K, giving T=60 °C under the supplied model.
simple.given: A device has a constant 120 W heater in a room at 20 °C. Its supplied loss model is P_loss=k<sub>loss</sub>(T−20), with k<sub>loss</sub>=3.0 W/K.
simple.find: Find the predicted steady device temperature.

challenge.title: What the initial slope fixes
challenge.problem: A heater and thermometer are embedded in a metal block. A student records the initial temperature slope just after switching on electrical heating. Explain what an initial-slope estimate of c improves and which errors still need checking.
steps: A small initial difference from room temperature reduces the room-loss correction.
The apparatus still warms, so its heat capacity must be included or independently calibrated.
Sensor lag, poor contact and internal temperature gradients can make the recorded slope differ from the mean block slope; compare heating/cooling data and repeat measurements.
challenge.answer: The initial slope reduces one loss error; it does not remove apparatus or temperature-measurement errors.
challenge.given: A heater and thermometer are embedded in a metal block. A student records the initial temperature slope just after switching on electrical heating.
challenge.find: Explain what an initial-slope estimate of c improves and which errors still need checking.

formula_cards.watch: A straight-line fit or short insulation trial supports a model only over its measured range and geometry. Separate conduction, convection, radiation and thermal bridges before generalising.
background: Steady temperature means zero change in stored energy, even while energy flows through the device. A cooling trace has a negative temperature slope; at the same temperature and unchanged surroundings it can estimate the loss that also occurs during heating.

A linear heat-loss model is an empirical approximation over a specified range. Its whole-device coefficient k<sub>loss</sub> has units W/K. Material conductivity k<sub>cond</sub> has units W/(m K); they describe different quantities.

Electrical potential difference V is energy transferred per coulomb, in volts, and current I is charge per second, in amperes. Thus VI is input power in watts and VIt is energy in joules for constant V and I. The input can warm apparatus as well as the specimen and replace environmental losses.

model_routine.title: Seven-step heat problem routine
steps: Draw the system boundary and mark every energy pathway crossing it.
Identify each material, phase, mass, temperature and apparatus heat capacity.
Split the process into sensible-heating, latent-heat and steady-transfer stages.
Test the possible final phase before solving for equilibrium temperature.
For steady transfer, reduce series and parallel paths and add conduction, convection and radiation losses.
For graphs and experiments, use net power, slopes, plateaux, calibration and cooling data.
Check units, signs, limiting cases, neglected pathways and whether the result fits the tested model range.

lesson.introduction_heading: Energy can change temperature, phase or both

introduction.title: Temperature and stored energy
introduction.body: Temperature tells us which way heat will flow when bodies interact. Internal energy is the microscopic energy stored in a chosen sample; it depends on material, amount, temperature and phase.

introduction.title: Choose the boundary
introduction.body: Name the objects inside your energy account. Include a cup, heater or thermometer when its energy storage matters. Heat crosses a boundary because of temperature difference; electrical work can also transfer energy into the system.

introduction.title: Read the thermal journey
introduction.body: Within one phase, energy usually changes temperature. During a pure substance’s melting or boiling at fixed pressure, energy can change the amount in each phase while temperature stays at the transition value.

lesson.symbol_heading: Distinguish energy, heat capacity and heat-transfer rate

items.name: Temperature
items.meaning: T is an absolute temperature in radiation equations. θ labels a Celsius temperature when that distinction matters.

items.name: Temperature change or difference
items.meaning: Δ means change. For heating use final minus initial; for a positive heat-loss magnitude use hot minus cold. A difference of 1 °C equals 1 K.
items.unit: K; a Celsius interval has the same number

items.name: Internal energy and its change
items.meaning: U is stored microscopic energy. ΔU is the change for the defined system.

items.name: Transferred energy
items.meaning: Q usually denotes heat transferred because of temperature difference. E can include electrical input; both are energy quantities.

items.name: Mass and elapsed time
items.meaning: Use kilograms with the listed specific thermal properties and seconds with watts.

symbol_groups.title: How much energy and how quickly?

items.name: Specific heat capacity
items.meaning: Energy needed for 1 kg to change temperature by 1 K within one phase; assumed constant over the stated range.

items.name: Heat capacity of a whole object
items.meaning: C=mc for one uniform material; a calibrated apparatus C may include several parts. Upper-case C already includes the amount of material.

items.name: Specific latent heats
items.meaning: f labels fusion (melting/freezing); v labels vaporisation (boiling/condensation). These are positive energy-per-mass magnitudes.
items.unit: J kg⁻¹, or kJ kg⁻¹ if all energies use kJ

items.name: Power or heat-transfer rate
items.meaning: Energy transferred each second; labels in, loss and net identify different pathways. This P means power here.

items.name: Temperature slope
items.meaning: Instantaneous temperature change per second, read from a graph tangent. It is positive while warming and negative while cooling; no calculus calculation is needed here.

items.name: Efficiency
items.meaning: Greek eta: useful output energy divided by supplied input energy. Multiply by 100 to report a percentage.

items.name: Conduction quantities
items.meaning: Thermal conductivity describes the material; A is the area perpendicular to heat flow and ℓ is layer thickness along the heat-flow path. ℓ avoids confusing thickness with latent heat L.
items.unit: k<sub>cond</sub>: W m⁻¹ K⁻¹; A: m²; ℓ: m

items.name: Thermal resistance
items.meaning: Temperature difference per watt of steady heat flow through a path. This is thermal resistance, not the gas constant used in Gas.

items.name: Emissivity and radiation constant
items.meaning: Greek epsilon is the surface’s thermal emissivity (0 to 1); sigma is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, 5.67×10⁻⁸.
items.unit: ε: no unit; σ: W m⁻² K⁻⁴

items.name: Surroundings temperature
items.meaning: The effective uniform surroundings temperature in the stated radiation-exchange model.

items.name: Overall linear loss coefficient
items.meaning: A fitted whole-device power loss per kelvin above the room. Some questions call this k; its W/K unit distinguishes it from material conductivity.

learning_map.big_idea: Follow energy across a chosen boundary. Decide whether each transfer changes temperature, changes phase, or leaves through another pathway.

basics.title: Temperature is a state; heat is a transfer
basics.story: Temperature tells the direction of thermal transfer. Internal energy is energy stored microscopically in a sample. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
basics.why: Two samples at the same temperature need not store equal internal energy. In a well-defined energy account, the change of stored energy equals all energy in minus all energy out.
basics.symbols: U and E: energy (J); Δ means final minus initial. Electrical work is another energy-transfer route.

basics.title: Heating within one phase changes temperature
basics.story: When no phase change occurs, the energy needed depends on mass, the material’s specific heat capacity and the temperature rise.
basics.why: Specific heat capacity tells how many joules heat 1 kg by 1 K. The product mc is the heat capacity of the whole sample.
basics.symbols: Q: transferred energy (J); m: mass (kg); c: specific heat capacity (J/(kg K)); ΔT: temperature change (K or °C).

basics.title: A phase change uses energy without the same temperature rise
basics.story: During melting at the melting point, energy changes the particle arrangement. For a pure substance at fixed pressure, solid and liquid can coexist at the transition temperature.
basics.why: After using energy to warm ice to its melting point, check whether enough energy remains to melt all of it before calculating a final liquid temperature.
basics.symbols: L: specific latent heat (J/kg); m: mass that changes phase (kg); Q: energy absorbed or released (J).

basics.title: Transfer pathways determine the energy balance
basics.story: Conduction transfers energy through interactions in matter; convection transports it with moving fluid; radiation transfers it through electromagnetic waves.
basics.why: An object can stay at constant temperature while energy flows through it: its input and output powers match. Insulation reduces transfer; it does not create energy.
basics.symbols: Power is transferred energy per second: 1 W=1 J/s. In E=Pt, E is energy (J), P is constant power (W) and t is time (s).

routes.title: Identify what the energy does
routes.cue: A heater warms a sample or a heating curve contains a plateau.
routes.connection: Separate temperature change from phase change before combining steps.

routes.title: Combine objects and transfer routes
routes.cue: Warm and cold materials interact, or energy crosses several layers.
routes.connection: Choose the system boundary, allow for the apparatus and losses, then test the phase and steady-state assumptions.

routes.title: Infer models from measurements
routes.cue: Radiation, cooling curves or unknown losses affect the observations.
routes.connection: Add the stated transfer law, define its range of validity and ask whether independent evidence separates competing explanations.

learning_map.checkpoint: Before doing arithmetic, can you draw the energy pathways and state which temperature or phase changes are possible?

easy.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy gained by the water.
easy.hint: Identify the temperature change of the water, then use its mass and specific heat.
easy.feedback_correct: Correct. The sample heat capacity is 2100 J/K; 30 K therefore requires 63000 J. The absorbed energy is positive.
easy.feedback_incorrect: Use the temperature change of 30 K, not the final temperature of 50 °C.
easy.explanation: The temperature rise is 50−20=30 °C, numerically 30 K. Q=mcΔT=0.50 kg × 4200 J/(kg K) × 30 K=63000 J. Convert using 1000 J=1 kJ: Q=63 kJ.
easy.context: A 0.50 kg sample of water is warmed from 20 °C to 50 °C. Take c_water=4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
easy.given: A 0.50 kg sample of water is warmed from 20 °C to 50 °C. Take c_water=4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
easy.find: Calculate the thermal energy gained by the water.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Heating within one liquid phase
worked_solution.model: The water stays liquid. Use its constant specific heat and its own temperature rise to calculate absorbed energy.
steps: The temperature rise is 50−20=30 °C, numerically 30 K.
Convert using 1000 J=1 kJ: Q=63 kJ.
worked_solution.check: The sample heat capacity is 2100 J/K; 30 K therefore requires 63000 J. The absorbed energy is positive.
worked_solution.common_error: Use the temperature change of 30 K, not the final temperature of 50 °C.

options: Both cups have the same internal energy because their temperatures are equal.
Cup B generally has more internal energy because it contains more water at the same temperature.
Cup A has more internal energy because its particles move faster.
Temperature measures the total energy in a sample.
easy.hint: Compare the amount of material after noting that temperature and substance match.
easy.feedback_correct: Correct. A shared temperature can coexist with different total stored energies.
easy.feedback_incorrect: Temperature is not a count of the sample’s total energy.
easy.explanation: Equal temperatures mean the cups would be in thermal equilibrium with each other; there is no reason for A’s particles to move faster. Cup B has 500/100=5 times the water mass. For the same material and state, internal energy relative to the same reference scales with amount. Choose Option 2: B has more internal energy. Options 1 and 4 confuse total stored energy with temperature, while Option 3 invents a temperature difference.
easy.context: Cup A contains 100 g of water at 40 °C. Cup B contains 500 g of water at 40 °C.
easy.given: Cup A contains 100 g of water at 40 °C. Cup B contains 500 g of water at 40 °C.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Temperature versus total internal energy
worked_solution.model: Compare the same material and liquid phase at the same temperature using one common energy reference. The larger sample contains more material.
steps: Equal temperatures mean the cups would be in thermal equilibrium with each other; there is no reason for A’s particles to move faster.
Cup B has 500/100=5 times the water mass. For the same material and state, internal energy relative to the same reference scales with amount.
Choose Option 2: B has more internal energy. Options 1 and 4 confuse total stored energy with temperature, while Option 3 invents a temperature difference.
worked_solution.final_answer: Option 2: Cup B generally has more internal energy because it contains more water at the same temperature.
worked_solution.check: A shared temperature can coexist with different total stored energies.
worked_solution.common_error: Temperature is not a count of the sample’s total energy.

easy.hint: Use the insulated boundary to equate energy released and absorbed; the equal heat capacities cancel.
easy.feedback_correct: Correct. Both portions change by 30 K in opposite directions, so their equal heat capacities transfer equal energy.
easy.feedback_incorrect: A simple average works here because both heat capacities are equal; it is not a rule for every mixture.
easy.explanation: Let the common final temperature be T. The hot sample releases mc(80−T); the cold sample absorbs mc(T−20). Set these positive energy magnitudes equal and cancel mc: 80−T=T−20. Solve 2T=100, so T=50 °C. This lies between the starting temperatures.
easy.context: Equal masses of water at 80 °C and 20 °C are mixed in an insulated container. The cup heat capacity and environmental heat exchange are negligible; take the same constant c for both samples.
easy.given: Equal masses of water at 80 °C and 20 °C are mixed in an insulated container. The cup heat capacity and environmental heat exchange are negligible; take the same constant c for both samples.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Mixing equal heat capacities
worked_solution.model: The two water portions form an insulated system with negligible cup storage. Equal mass and equal c give equal whole-sample heat capacities.
steps: Let the common final temperature be T. The hot sample releases mc(80−T); the cold sample absorbs mc(T−20).
Set these positive energy magnitudes equal and cancel mc: 80−T=T−20.
Solve 2T=100, so T=50 °C. This lies between the starting temperatures.
worked_solution.check: Both portions change by 30 K in opposite directions, so their equal heat capacities transfer equal energy.
worked_solution.common_error: A simple average works here because both heat capacities are equal; it is not a rule for every mixture.

easy.prompt: What happens to the supplied energy during the horizontal section of the graph?
options: It disappears because temperature is constant.
It increases particle kinetic energy only.
It increases particle potential energy as the solid melts.
It reduces the mass of the sample.
easy.hint: Separate a change of phase from a rise of temperature.
easy.feedback_correct: Correct. Energy can enter throughout the plateau even though ΔT is zero.
easy.feedback_incorrect: Q=mcΔT is not the model for the phase-changing part of the journey.
easy.explanation: On the horizontal graph segment, temperature is constant, so energy input is not producing a sensible temperature rise. During melting, microscopic arrangement changes and the liquid fraction increases; the supplied latent energy increases the relevant microscopic potential energy. Choose Option 3. Energy is conserved, mean thermal motion is not rising as in single-phase heating, and no mass-loss mechanism is stated.
easy.context: A solid is heated at constant power. Its temperature rises, remains constant for several minutes, then rises again. The sample is pure, its mass is constant and heating is at fixed pressure with negligible loss; the plateau is melting.
easy.given: A solid is heated at constant power. Its temperature rises, remains constant for several minutes, then rises again. The sample is pure, its mass is constant and heating is at fixed pressure with negligible loss; the plateau is melting.
easy.find: What happens to the supplied energy during the horizontal section of the graph?

worked_solution.tested_idea: Latent energy during melting
worked_solution.model: The stated plateau is a pure-sample melting interval at fixed pressure with continuing energy input.
steps: On the horizontal graph segment, temperature is constant, so energy input is not producing a sensible temperature rise.
During melting, microscopic arrangement changes and the liquid fraction increases; the supplied latent energy increases the relevant microscopic potential energy.
Choose Option 3. Energy is conserved, mean thermal motion is not rising as in single-phase heating, and no mass-loss mechanism is stated.
worked_solution.final_answer: Option 3: It increases particle potential energy as the solid melts.
worked_solution.check: Energy can enter throughout the plateau even though ΔT is zero.
worked_solution.common_error: Q=mcΔT is not the model for the phase-changing part of the journey.

easy.prompt: Calculate the energy gained by the aluminium.
easy.hint: Use the aluminium value of c and the difference between its two temperatures.
easy.feedback_correct: Correct. The energy is positive and scales with both the block mass and the 50 K rise.
easy.feedback_incorrect: Do not use the water specific heat for an aluminium sample.
easy.explanation: The rise is ΔT=75−25=50 K. The block heat capacity is mc=0.80×900=720 J/K. Energy absorbed is 720×50=36000 J=36 kJ.
easy.context: A 0.80 kg aluminium block with c=900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ is warmed from 25 °C to 75 °C.
