formula_cards.title: Electron shells and periodic position
background: A shell is an allowed electron energy level. Use 2,8,8,2 as a restricted filling pattern for the first 20 neutral atoms: fill the first shell to 2, the next to 8, and continue as in the examples. These numbers do not state the maximum capacity of every shell in all atoms.

A period is a horizontal row; its number gives the occupied-shell count of a ground-state neutral atom. A group is a vertical column. Valence electrons are outer-shell electrons. For the main groups used here, groups 1 and 2 have 1 and 2 valence electrons; groups 13–18 have 3–8. Helium is the group 18 exception with only 2 electrons.

Group 1 commonly forms 1+ions, group 2 forms 2+ions, and group 17 forms 1−ions. A closed outer shell often accompanies a stable simple ion. Use the stated simple-ion model; not every element forms every charge suggested by an octet. Ion formation changes the electron count, not the element’s period or Z.

simple.title: Sodium
simple.given: A neutral sodium atom has Z=11.
simple.find: Give its shell pattern and common ion.
steps: There are 11 electrons.
Place 2 in the first shell and 8 in the second: 2,8,1.
Losing the outer electron gives Na⁺ with 2,8.

challenge.title: Compare two neighbours
challenge.given: Neutral X has Z=12; neutral Y has Z=17.
steps: X is 2,8,2 and commonly loses two electrons to form X²⁺.
Y is 2,8,7 and commonly gains one to form Y⁻.
Charge balance then requires one X²⁺ per two Y⁻; shells predict a tendency, not an isotope mass.
challenge.answer: X²⁺ and Y⁻; empirical formula XY₂.

formula_cards.watch: Count shells for the neutral atom when finding its periodic-table position. Na⁺ has two occupied shells but sodium remains a period 3 element.

formula_cards.title: Periodic trends: attraction, size and electron removal
formula_cards.focus: MODEL · explain the trend before predicting
background: Positive nuclei attract electrons. Inner electrons partly shield outer electrons from that attraction. Across a main-group period, added protons increase attraction within the same outer shell: atomic radius generally decreases. Down a group, extra occupied shells place outer electrons farther away and add shielding: radius generally increases.

First ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove the first electron from a gaseous neutral atom; molar values use kJ/mol. It generally rises across a period and falls down a group. Stronger attraction makes removal harder. These are broad trends with exceptions, not an exact ranking of every neighbouring pair.

After a main-group metal loses its outer electrons, its cation is usually smaller than the neutral atom. An anion is usually larger than its neutral atom. Comparing ions with the same electron count isolates nuclear attraction: more protons usually pull the shared electron cloud closer.

simple.title: One extra shell
simple.given: Lithium has neutral shell pattern 2,1; sodium has 2,8,1.
simple.find: Predict which neutral atom is larger and more easily loses its outer electron.
simple.problem: Lithium has neutral shell pattern 2,1; sodium has 2,8,1. Predict which neutral atom is larger and more easily loses its outer electron.
steps: Both are group 1 atoms with one valence electron.
Sodium has an extra occupied shell; its outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded.
The general trends predict larger sodium and easier removal of its outer electron. More protons alone do not decide a down-group comparison.
simple.answer: Sodium is generally larger and has lower first ionisation energy.

challenge.title: Same electron count, different nuclei
challenge.given: P⁺ has 11 protons and 10 electrons; Q²⁺ has 12 protons and 10 electrons.
challenge.find: Predict the smaller ion and explain why.
challenge.problem: P⁺ has 11 protons and 10 electrons; Q²⁺ has 12 protons and 10 electrons. Predict the smaller ion and explain why.
steps: Both ions have ten electrons with shell pattern 2,8.
Q²⁺ has one extra proton attracting the same number of electrons.
The stronger nuclear attraction contracts that cloud more; compare these equal-electron-count ions rather than using only the charge labels.
challenge.answer: Q²⁺ is smaller in the stated main-group model.

formula_cards.watch: Do not compare neutral atoms and ions as if their electron counts and occupied shells were unchanged.

figures.title: Two different comparisons
figures.alt: Across a main-group period: same occupied-shell count, stronger nuclear attraction, generally smaller radius. Down a group: extra occupied shells and shielding, generally larger radius.
figures.caption: Qualitative trends; circles are schematic, not measured atomic radii.

formula_cards.title: Chemical bonds explain properties
background: An ionic bond is electrostatic attraction between opposite charges in an extended lattice. Electron transfer creates ions; attraction holds the lattice together. A salt formula gives the simplest ion ratio, not a separate salt molecule.

A covalent bond has shared electron density attracted to both positive nuclei. Simple molecular substances contain separate molecules; giant covalent substances have a connected network. Melting a molecular solid usually overcomes attractions between molecules while preserving the covalent bonds within them.

Electrical conduction needs mobile charged particles. Ions are held at lattice sites in a typical ionic solid; molten ions can move. Dissolved ionic material conducts when mobile ions are present. A metal has mobile electrons in both solid and liquid states.

Many molecular substances melt at relatively low temperatures and conduct poorly. Many giant covalent networks have high melting points; diamond insulates, while graphite conducts. Use several observations and their conditions together: neither melting point nor conductivity alone uniquely identifies a substance.

simple.title: One material
simple.given: A pure salt does not conduct while solid but conducts when molten.
steps: The solid lattice holds charged ions at fixed sites.
Melting allows ions to move through the sample.
The charge carriers are moving ions; producing new electrons is unnecessary.
simple.answer: Mobile ions carry current after melting.

challenge.title: Separate models
challenge.given: P has a high melting point and conducts only when molten. Q has a high melting point and is insulating in both states.
steps: P fits an ionic lattice with mobile ions in the melt.
Q could fit an insulating network structure.
High melting point alone does not establish ionic bonding; additional chemical evidence is needed.
challenge.answer: Ionic P supported; Q remains a different candidate.

formula_cards.watch: A full outer shell helps describe a simple-ion tendency. Electrostatic attraction explains the bond; the phrase “wants eight electrons” does not explain a force.

figures.title: Structure and charge carriers
figures.alt: Ionic solid: positive and negative ions in a lattice. Molecular solid: separate bonded molecules. Metal: positive ion cores surrounded by mobile electrons.
figures.caption: Models of structure and charge motion. Drawings are schematic and do not show real sizes.

formula_cards.title: Radioactivity and nuclear bookkeeping
background: Radioactive decay changes an unstable nucleus. The original nucleus is the parent; the resulting nucleus is the daughter and may itself be unstable. A nuclear change can alter the element when Z changes. Chemical ion formation rearranges electrons without changing Z.

Alpha (α) emission removes two protons and two neutrons: daughter A decreases by 4 and Z by 2. Beta-minus (β⁻) decay converts a neutron into a proton and emits an electron: daughter A is unchanged and Z increases by 1. The beta electron is produced in the nuclear process; it is not an electron stripped from an outer shell.

Gamma (γ) emission releases nuclear energy as a photon (a packet of electromagnetic energy); A and Z are unchanged. For these questions, track daughter A and Z at each step, then find neutron count A−Z. A stated rapid chain is a bookkeeping model, not a claim that every such chain occurs naturally.

Alpha radiation usually has low penetration; gamma is much more penetrating. Penetration depends on radiation energy and shielding material. Ionising radiation can remove electrons from matter; the course uses prepared data, with no radioactive-source handling.

simple.title: One alpha emission
simple.given: A parent nucleus has A=238 and Z=92 and emits one alpha particle.
simple.find: Find daughter A, Z and neutron count.
simple.problem: A parent nucleus has A=238 and Z=92 and emits one alpha particle. Find daughter A, Z and neutron count.
steps: The emitted helium nucleus carries 4 nucleons, including 2 protons.
The daughter therefore has A=238−4=234 and Z=92−2=90.
Its neutron count is 234−90=144; the parent had 146, so two neutrons left in the alpha particle.

challenge.title: A stated decay sequence
challenge.given: In a hypothetical bookkeeping sequence, a nucleus starts at A=220,Z=88 and undergoes one alpha, one beta-minus and one gamma emission.
challenge.find: Find the final heavy daughter’s proton and neutron counts.
challenge.problem: In a hypothetical bookkeeping sequence, a nucleus starts at A=220,Z=88 and undergoes one alpha, one beta-minus and one gamma emission. Find the final heavy daughter’s proton and neutron counts.
steps: After alpha emission: A=216 and Z=86.
Beta-minus converts one neutron into a proton: A stays 216 and Z becomes 87. Gamma changes neither count.
The final heavy daughter has 87 protons and 216−87=129 neutrons. Do not include the emitted particles as part of that daughter.

formula_cards.watch: Losing an outer electron makes a positive ion without changing Z. Beta-minus decay changes Z because a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton.

figures.title: What changes in the daughter nucleus?
figures.alt: Alpha: A decreases by 4,Z by 2. Beta-minus: A unchanged,Z increases by 1. Gamma: neither count changes.
figures.caption: These are nucleus-count changes; electron-shell changes are a separate question.

formula_cards.title: Half-life and detector background
formula_cards.focus: MODEL · remaining parents and measured counts
background: Half-life h is the interval in which the expected undecayed parent population halves. Decay times of individual nuclei are random; the law predicts a large-population mean. N₀ is the initial parent count, N the expected remaining count after time t. Use the same time unit for t and h; N is not a neutron count.

A detector records only some emissions. R is the measured count rate and B is a constant background count rate, both in the same unit such as counts/min. Subtract background before comparing source rates. With unchanged geometry and detection efficiency, and no additional changing signal, the corrected source rate follows the same halving pattern.

The fraction that has decayed is one minus the fraction remaining. A stable daughter retained in the sample is still a nucleus, so the total retained heavy-nucleus count need not fall when the parent population falls. State which population a requested mean or fraction uses.

formulas.meaning: Large-population radioactive decay at constant half-life.
symbols: N₀,N: undecayed nucleus counts; t,h: same time unit.

formulas.meaning: Subtract the fixed background before inferring a source half-life.
symbols: R: measured rate; B: constant background; R_source: source contribution. All use the same unit, e.g. counts/min.

simple.title: Two half-lives
simple.given: A sample has 800 undecayed nuclei and half-life 3 h.
simple.find: Find the expected undecayed count after 6 h.
steps: Six hours is two half-lives.
Halve twice: 800→400→200.
Three quarters decayed; one quarter remains.

challenge.title: Subtract background
challenge.given: A detector reads 220 counts/min initially and 70 after 4 h. Constant background is 20 counts/min.
steps: Source signals are 200 and 50, not 220 and 70.
The source signal falls to one quarter in 4 h.
Two half-lives take 4 h, so h=2 h.

formula_cards.watch: Halve the source signal, not the source-plus-background reading. Retained daughters are not undecayed parents.

figures.title: Measured rate includes background
figures.alt: Measured rates 220,120,70 counts/min at 0,2,4 h include constant background 20 counts/min. Source-only rates are 200,100,50.
figures.caption: Calculated illustration for a 2 h half-life; not measured student or laboratory data.

formula_cards.title: Isotopes and weighted means
background: Isotopes share Z but have different neutron numbers and masses. Their ordinary chemistry is similar because their electron structures are similar.

Relative atomic mass Aᵣ compares an atom-number-weighted mean mass with the atomic mass unit u. A measured mean expressed in u has the same numerical value as Aᵣ. Equal masses of different isotopes do not contain equal numbers of atoms.

formulas.meaning: Use atom-number fractions fᵢ (sum 1) and isotope relative masses mᵢ. Aᵣ has no unit.
symbols: fᵢ: fraction of atoms in isotope i; mᵢ: its mass in units of u; Aᵣ: dimensionless weighted relative mass. Σ means sum over isotopes.

formulas.meaning: Amount n in mol equals mass m divided by matching molar mass M.
symbols: n: amount in mol; m: sample mass in g; M: molar mass of that substance in g/mol.

simple.title: Atom fractions
simple.given: 60% of atoms have isotope mass 10 u; 40% have mass 11 u.
simple.problem: 60% of atoms have isotope mass 10 u; 40% have mass 11 u. Find mean mass.
steps: Convert atom percentages to 0.60 and 0.40.

challenge.title: Equal masses
challenge.given: Equal sample masses of isotope-10 and isotope-11 are mixed.
challenge.problem: Equal sample masses of isotope-10 and isotope-11 are mixed. Find the isotope-11 atom fraction.
steps: Atom amounts are proportional to 1/10 and 1/11.
Normalise the isotope-11 amount: (1/11)/(1/10+1/11).

formula_cards.watch: Weight by numbers of atoms. For equal-mass portions, first convert each mass into an amount.

formula_cards.title: Moles, mass and formula composition
background: A mole is a counting unit: one mole contains exactly 6.02214076×10²³ entities; these questions use 6.02×10²³. Specify atoms, molecules, ions or formula units.

Molar mass M is the mass of one mole, typically g/mol. A formula’s subscripts tell how many atoms contribute to its mass. An empirical formula gives the simplest atom ratio; molecular mass determines how many empirical units are in one molecule.

formulas.meaning: Amount n in mol equals mass m divided by matching molar mass M.
symbols: n: amount in mol; m: sample mass in g; M: molar mass of that substance in g/mol.

formulas.meaning: N_A≈6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹ counts specified entities per mole; name the entity.
symbols: N: number of the named entity; n: mol of that entity; N_A≈6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹.

formulas.meaning: Mass fraction w becomes mass percent after multiplying by 100.
symbols: w: mass fraction, no unit; both masses use the same unit. Multiply by 100 for %.

simple.title: Mass to particles
simple.given: 5.85 g NaCl has M=58.5 g/mol and fully separates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in water.
simple.problem: 5.85 g NaCl has M=58.5 g/mol and fully separates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in water. Count dissolved ions.
steps: n=5.85/58.5=0.100 mol of NaCl formula units.
Each unit supplies two ions, giving 0.200 mol of ions.

challenge.title: From mass composition
challenge.given: A compound contains C:H:O in mass ratio 12:2:16; M=180 g/mol.
challenge.problem: A compound contains C:H:O in mass ratio 12:2:16; M=180 g/mol. Find its molecular formula.
steps: Divide by atomic molar masses 12,1,16: atom ratio 1:2:1.
CH₂O has molar mass 30 g/mol.
180/30=6 empirical units.

formula_cards.watch: Compare moles of atoms to obtain atom ratios; mass ratios are generally different.

formula_cards.title: Separation and chromatography evidence
background: Solute is the dissolved substance; solvent is the dissolving medium. Filtration traps insoluble particles but dissolved salt passes through. Evaporation/crystallisation recovers dissolved solid; distillation can collect a volatile liquid.

Chromatography carries components in a moving solvent over a stationary material. Different relative attractions give different travel distances. Rf is meaningful only for specified solvent and experimental conditions.

formulas.meaning: Distances measured from the same baseline along the solvent travel direction.
symbols: d_spot,d_front: distances from one baseline in matching units; Rf has no unit.

formulas.meaning: Recovery measures how much of the original target material is collected; it differs from product purity.
symbols: Numerator: collected target mass; denominator: original target mass, in the same unit.

simple.title: Travel ratio
simple.given: A spot travels 5.2 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm.
simple.problem: A spot travels 5.2 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm. Find Rf.
steps: Measure both from the starting line.
Divide 5.2/8.0.

challenge.title: Recovery versus purity
challenge.given: A mixture initially contains 10 g salt; 8.5 g pure salt is collected.
challenge.problem: A mixture initially contains 10 g salt; 8.5 g pure salt is collected. Find recovery and product purity.
steps: Recovery compares collected salt with initial salt: 8.5/10.
The collected product is stated to contain only salt.

formula_cards.watch: One spot does not prove purity: two components can overlap in one solvent. A matching Rf supports, but does not establish, identity.

figures.title: Chromatogram distances
figures.alt: A paper strip with a shared baseline, solvent front and solute spot.
figures.caption: Original BEN Science schematic; use the stated data, not the drawing scale.

formula_cards.title: Density, pores and reliable comparisons
background: Density compares mass with a defined volume. One mL equals one cm³. Material density uses the solid material volume; bulk density uses external volume including pores.

Repeated values describe precision. An independent standard checks calibration and accuracy. A matching density or chromatographic spot alone does not uniquely identify a substance. Main-group elements often share outer-electron patterns and analogous formulas; masses and reaction rates can differ.

formulas.meaning: Density uses the sample mass and the volume defined by the measurement.
symbols: ρ: density; m: mass; V: explicitly defined sample volume. Common units: kg/m³ or g/cm³.

formulas.meaning: Mass fraction w becomes mass percent after multiplying by 100.
symbols: w: mass fraction, no unit; both masses use the same unit. Multiply by 100 for %.

simple.title: Displacement
simple.given: A 54 g impermeable object raises water from 30 to 48 mL.
simple.problem: A 54 g impermeable object raises water from 30 to 48 mL. Find density.
steps: Object volume=48−30=18 mL=18 cm³.

challenge.title: Pore accounting
challenge.given: Dry mass=84 g; material density=3 g/cm³; external volume=40 cm³. Saturation adds 6 g of water of density 1 g/cm³.
challenge.problem: Dry mass=84 g; material density=3 g/cm³; external volume=40 cm³. Saturation adds 6 g of water of density 1 g/cm³. Find closed-pore volume.
steps: Solid material occupies 84/3=28 cm³; total pores=40−28=12 cm³.
Absorbed water occupies 6 cm³ of open pores.
Closed pores=12−6.

formula_cards.watch: For same-group trends: Group 1 generally becomes more reactive down the group, while Group 17 generally becomes less reactive. State the group and reaction rather than a universal rule.

mastery_targets.title: Atomic identity and electric charge
mastery_targets.body: Distinguish protons, neutrons and electrons; separate ion formation, isotope change and nuclear decay.

mastery_targets.title: Shell structure and periodic reasoning
mastery_targets.body: Infer simple-ion tendencies and explain broad size/electron-removal trends using attraction, shielding and occupied shells.

mastery_targets.body: Explain conduction using mobile charges; distinguish lattice, molecular and network structures using multiple observations.

learning_map.big_idea: Keep identity, structure and amount separate. Nuclear composition defines the element; electrons and bonding explain many properties; mole-based counting connects particles to measured samples.

basics.title: The nucleus fixes elemental identity
basics.story: An atom contains a nucleus with protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons. Proton number defines the element. Isotopes of one element have different neutron numbers.
basics.why: Changing electrons makes an ion without changing the element. A nuclear change can change the element because proton number may change.
basics.symbols: Z: proton/atomic number; N_n: neutron count; A: mass number (protons plus neutrons); all are counts. A is not the relative atomic mass A_r.

basics.title: Electrons and bonds explain properties
basics.story: Outer electrons influence chemical reactions and bonding. Molecules contain bonded atoms; ionic solids form extended arrays of ions rather than separate molecules of the formula.
basics.why: Explain a measured property through the particles and interactions involved. Electrical conduction requires mobile charged particles, which differ between metals, solutions and solid ionic lattices.
basics.symbols: Ion: particle with net charge; cation: positive ion; anion: negative ion. A compound has chemically combined elements in a defined composition.

basics.title: Moles connect mass to numbers of entities
basics.story: A mole is an amount containing exactly 6.02214076×10²³ specified entities. Specify atoms, molecules or formula units before counting.
basics.why: Dividing sample mass by mass per mole gives moles. Multiply moles by the Avogadro constant to count the specified entities; multiply again by atoms per entity only if asked for atoms.
basics.symbols: n: amount (mol); m: mass (g if M uses g/mol); M: molar mass (g/mol). N: entity count; N_A=6.02214076×10²³ mol⁻¹.

basics.title: Measurements provide evidence about a sample
basics.story: A mixture contains multiple substances without a single fixed chemical composition. Separation, density, isotopic averages and detector readings each reveal different information.
basics.why: Use what the instrument actually measures: a chromatography spot is evidence under particular conditions, and a detector count may include background. Neither measurement alone identifies every feature of the sample.
basics.symbols: Relative atomic mass is an isotope-weighted mean, not the mass number of a single nucleus.

routes.title: Establish identity and structure
routes.cue: A task names atoms, ions, shells, bonds or nuclear changes.
routes.connection: Choose whether it concerns the nucleus, electrons or particle arrangement before counting.

routes.title: Translate between particles and measured composition

easy.given: Neutral atoms P,Q,R have shell patterns P:2,8,1; Q:2,8,2; R:2,8,8,1. Use the broad main-group radius trends in the Concept Brief.
easy.find: Which prediction and explanation are supported?
options: R is generally larger than P because it has an extra occupied shell; Q is generally smaller than P because its nucleus attracts the same-shell electrons more strongly.
R is smaller than P because its nucleus contains more protons; shielding and shell count can be ignored.
P and Q must have equal radii because they occupy the same number of shells.
R and P must have equal radii because both have one outer electron.
easy.hint: Compare occupied shells first, then nuclear attraction for atoms in the same period.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Explain two different periodic radius trends
worked_solution.model: Use the stated neutral shell patterns, then distinguish an added shell from a stronger nucleus within the same shell.
steps: The patterns give proton/electron counts P=11,Q=12,R=19. P and Q have three occupied shells; R has four.
R and P each have one valence electron, but R’s extra occupied shell places its outer electron farther out with more shielding. R is generally larger.
Q and P use the same outer shell. Q has an extra proton, so stronger net attraction generally makes Q smaller.
Option 1 fits both explanations. The other options ignore either occupied shells, shielding or changing attraction.
worked_solution.final_answer: Option 1: R generally larger than P; Q generally smaller than P.
worked_solution.check: Same group means similar valence patterns, not identical radii. Same period means the same occupied-shell count, not identical attraction.
worked_solution.common_error: Using proton number alone for a down-group comparison, or assuming one valence electron fixes the atomic size.

test.given: In a hypothetical nuclear bookkeeping model, a large population initially contains only nuclei with A=232 and Z=90. Each original nucleus has half-life 6.00 h. Once it decays, a rapid chain completes exactly two alpha and two beta-minus decays and leaves one daughter treated as stable over this observation interval; intermediate lifetimes are negligible. All final heavy nuclei are retained and alpha particles leave the sample. Consider only original or final daughter heavy nuclei, not emitted particles.
test.context: In a hypothetical nuclear bookkeeping model, a large population initially contains only nuclei with A=232 and Z=90. Each original nucleus has half-life 6.00 h. Once it decays, a rapid chain completes exactly two alpha and two beta-minus decays and leaves one daughter treated as stable over this observation interval; intermediate lifetimes are negligible. All final heavy nuclei are retained and alpha particles leave the sample. Consider only original or final daughter heavy nuclei, not emitted particles.
test.find: Find the mean proton count per retained heavy nucleus after 12.0 h. Give the result to one decimal place.
test.prompt: Find the mean proton count per retained heavy nucleus after 12.0 h. Give the result to one decimal place.
test.hint: First track A and Z through the stated completed chain; separately find the fractions of parents and final daughters after two half-lives.
test.feedback_correct: The mean lies between 88 and 90; it is a population mean, not the proton count of an individual nucleus.
test.feedback_incorrect: Do not average only the daughters or count emitted alpha particles as retained heavy nuclei.
test.explanation: Let the initial number of parent nuclei be N₀. Two alpha emissions remove 8 nucleons and 4 protons, so the completed daughter chain has A=232−8=224 and Z=90−4+2=88 after the two beta-minus conversions. Neutron count is 224−88=136. Twelve hours is 12/6=2 parent half-lives. The undecayed parents are N₀/4; the fraction completing the stated rapid chain is 3/4. Intermediate nuclei do not accumulate under the given model. Each initial parent leaves one retained heavy nucleus: either an undecayed parent with 90 protons or a final daughter with 88 protons. The denominator remains N₀; emitted alpha and beta particles are excluded. Mean proton count per retained heavy nucleus=(0.25 N₀×90+0.75 N₀×88)/N₀=88.5.

Twelve hours is 12/6=2 parent half-lives. The undecayed parents are N₀/4; the fraction completing the stated rapid chain is 3/4. Intermediate nuclei do not accumulate under the given model.

Each initial parent leaves one retained heavy nucleus: either an undecayed parent with 90 protons or a final daughter with 88 protons. The denominator remains N₀; emitted alpha and beta particles are excluded.
Mean proton count per retained heavy nucleus=(0.25 N₀×90+0.75 N₀×88)/N₀=88.5.
worked_solution.check: The mean lies between 88 and 90. For 100 initial parents,25 remain and 75 become daughters:2250+6600=8850 protons in 100 retained heavy nuclei, averaging 88.5.

topics.title: Chemical Reactions and Conservation
knowledge_points: mass, gas volume, yield and purity

lesson.goal: Represent reactions as conserved particle rearrangements, use equation ratios to infer limiting quantities, and judge whether experimental evidence supports the proposed chemistry.
prerequisites: Week 6 atoms, ions, formulae and moles

formula_cards.title: Chemical change and closed-system conservation
background: A reaction changes which atoms are bonded together. Ordinary chemistry conserves each element’s atoms and the total charge. Melting changes arrangement and state without changing substance identity.

A balanced equation changes coefficients before whole formulas. A subscript is part of a substance’s identity and must stay fixed. Gas entering or leaving makes an open vessel’s mass change; include that gas in a complete balance.

formulas.meaning: Total mass is conserved for a closed chemical system; include gases and retained solids.
symbols: Both m values are total masses of the same closed system, including all gas, liquid and solid material.

simple.title: Balance atoms
simple.given: Al+O₂→Al₂O₃.
simple.problem: Al+O₂→Al₂O₃. Find the smallest whole-number coefficients.
steps: Two Al₂O₃ units contain 6 O atoms, requiring 3 O₂.
They contain 4 Al atoms, requiring coefficient 4.

challenge.title: Open vessel
challenge.given: 8 g metal combines with 2 g oxygen from air.
challenge.find: Find oxide mass and explain the gain.
challenge.problem: 8 g metal combines with 2 g oxygen from air. Find oxide mass and explain the gain.
steps: Include oxygen in the starting system: 8+2 g.
All atoms remain in the product if no material is lost.
challenge.answer: 10 g; oxygen entered the weighed vessel

formula_cards.watch: Bubbles, colour or temperature changes are evidence to investigate; one sign alone does not uniquely identify a reaction or gas.

formula_cards.title: Amount ratios and the limiting reactant
background: The coefficients specify numbers of reacting particles and mole amounts. They do not generally specify mass ratios. Convert masses to moles before using the balanced equation.

Compare each available amount divided by its coefficient. The smallest value is the maximum reaction extent. Use the extent to find every consumed and produced amount, then subtract consumption from the starting inventory.

formulas.meaning: Mass divided by molar mass gives amount of a named substance.
symbols: n: amount in mol; m: sample mass in g; M: molar mass of that substance in g/mol.

formulas.meaning: For aA+bB reacting, these are amounts consumed, not necessarily the initial amounts.
symbols: n_A,n_B: amounts consumed in mol; a,b: coefficients in the balanced equation.

formulas.meaning: The smaller available amount/coefficient limits the reaction. ξ is reaction extent in mol.
symbols: n_A,0 and n_B,0: initial amounts in mol; a,b: coefficients; ξ_max: greatest allowed reaction extent in mol; min means choose the smaller.

simple.title: Required hydrogen
simple.given: 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O; 7 O₂ molecules react.
simple.problem: 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O; 7 O₂ molecules react. Find required H₂ molecules.
steps: The coefficient ratio H₂:O₂ is 2:1.
Multiply 7 by 2.

challenge.title: Limiting amount
challenge.given: 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O; 8 mol H₂ and 3 mol O₂ are mixed.
challenge.problem: 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O; 8 mol H₂ and 3 mol O₂ are mixed. Find water and leftover hydrogen.
steps: Extents allowed are 8/2=4 mol and 3/1=3 mol.
Oxygen limits extent to 3 mol; water formed=2×3=6 mol.
Hydrogen left=8−2×3.

formula_cards.watch: Count only the limiting amount as reacting; being in the vessel does not mean all of a substance reacts.

formula_cards.title: Purity, yield and collection recovery
background: Purity compares target-compound mass with the whole starting sample. Theoretical yield assumes the stated chemistry and complete conversion of the limiting reactant. Actual yield may be smaller.
Collection recovery describes how much formed product reaches a measuring device. A low reading can reflect chemistry, collection loss or both. Independent calibration can separate these effects.

formulas.meaning: w is reactive mass fraction; inert impurities do not contribute to the specified reaction.
symbols: w: purity mass fraction, no unit; the two m quantities use the same mass unit.

formulas.meaning: Yield is a fraction; express percent by multiplying by 100. Separate chemical yield from collection recovery.
symbols: Y: yield fraction; actual and theoretical masses refer to the same product and unit.

simple.title: Reactive portion
simple.given: 20 g mineral is 80% reactive material and 20% inert.
simple.problem: 20 g mineral is 80% reactive material and 20% inert. Find reactive mass.
steps: Convert 80% to w=0.80.
Multiply 20×0.80.

challenge.title: Correct a collector
challenge.given: A collector reads 180 mL, recovers 90%, and theoretical production is 250 mL.
challenge.problem: A collector reads 180 mL, recovers 90%, and theoretical production is 250 mL. Find chemical yield.
steps: Produced volume=180/0.90=200 mL.
Compare production with theory: 200/250=0.80.

formula_cards.watch: A wet or impure product can give an apparent yield above 100%; verify identity and constant mass.

formula_cards.title: Gas amounts and multi-stage inventories
background: At the same temperature and pressure, gas volume is proportional to mole amount. A supplied molar volume V_m converts between them. Removing condensed water changes which species remain in the dry gas.

For a process with reaction, filtration, heating or recycle, label every stream. A separated filtrate is no longer available to later solid heating. Recycled material re-enters an inventory; it is never created for free.

formulas.meaning: V_m is gas volume per mole at the specified temperature and pressure.
symbols: V: gas volume in L; n: gas amount in mol; V_m: stated molar volume in L/mol.

formulas.meaning: A substance inventory tracks initial amount plus production minus consumption; include transfers between stages.
symbols: All n values are mol of one substance: final, initial, produced and consumed amounts. Add transfers when the boundary is open.

simple.title: Gas volume ratio
simple.given: 2CO+O₂→2CO₂; 30 mL O₂ reacts with excess CO, all gases compared at the same T and P.
simple.problem: 2CO+O₂→2CO₂; 30 mL O₂ reacts with excess CO, all gases compared at the same T and P. Find CO₂ volume.
steps: One volume O₂ produces two volumes CO₂.

challenge.title: Dry product gas
challenge.given: 4 L CH₄ and 6 L O₂ react by CH₄+2O₂→CO₂+2H₂O; all water is removed and remaining gases return to initial T and P.
challenge.problem: 4 L CH₄ and 6 L O₂ react by CH₄+2O₂→CO₂+2H₂O; all water is removed and remaining gases return to initial T and P. Find CO₂ fraction.
steps: O₂ permits 3 L CH₄ to react, leaving 1 L CH₄.
CO₂ volume is 3 L.
Dry total is 4 L, so CO₂ fraction=3/4.

formula_cards.watch: Volume coefficients apply only to gases at matching conditions; do not count removed liquid water as dry gas.

figures.title: Process boundaries
figures.alt: A reaction mixture passes through solid separation and heating while filtrate leaves the process.

formula_cards.title: Energy, activation barriers and catalysts
background: Reaction energy change compares final and initial states. Negative ΔH means energy is released; positive means absorbed. Activation energy measures the barrier above the starting side of a reaction.

A catalyst participates in intermediate steps and is regenerated after a full cycle. It can lower forward and reverse barriers, but leaves endpoint energies and the overall reaction energy change unchanged. Oxidation loses electrons; reduction gains them, so electron transfers balance.

formulas.meaning: Energy released to surroundings is a negative reaction energy change.
symbols: H values: energy levels per mol of the equation as written, in kJ/mol; Δ means final minus initial.

formulas.meaning: Activation energy is measured from the reactants of the chosen forward or reverse direction.
symbols: E_a: activation barrier; H_peak,H_start: peak and chosen starting-side levels, all in kJ/mol.

formulas.meaning: A calorimeter of total heat capacity C stores energy Q when its temperature rises ΔT.
symbols: Q: stored heat in J; C: total heat capacity in J/K; ΔT: temperature rise in K.

simple.title: Reaction profile
simple.given: Reactants are at 80 kJ/mol, products at 20 kJ/mol and the peak at 110 kJ/mol.
simple.find: Find forward ΔH and reverse activation energy.
simple.problem: Reactants are at 80 kJ/mol, products at 20 kJ/mol and the peak at 110 kJ/mol. Find forward ΔH and reverse activation energy.
steps: The reverse direction starts at products: E_a,reverse=110−20.

challenge.title: Catalyst cycles
challenge.given: A+B→C is achieved through M+A→MA and MA+B→M+C; 0.10 mol catalyst converts 0.30 mol A with excess B.
challenge.find: Find cycles per original catalyst particle.
challenge.problem: A+B→C is achieved through M+A→MA and MA+B→M+C; 0.10 mol catalyst converts 0.30 mol A with excess B. Find cycles per original catalyst particle.
steps: Add the equations: intermediate MA and regenerated M cancel.
Each full cycle forms one C; 0.30 mol cycles complete.
Mean cycles per catalyst particle=0.30/0.10.

formula_cards.watch: A catalyst is reused. Its initial amount need not equal the maximum amount of product.

formula_cards.title: Evidence, uncertainty and independent checks
background: A model must explain all observations under the stated conditions. Two independent measurements can distinguish product formed from product collected. A plateau alone may mean exhausted reagent, equilibrium, surface inhibition or an instrument limit.

A reported value ±u gives a stated uncertainty interval here. Compare predictions and readings with their uncertainties; a mismatch larger than allowed error challenges the account but does not uniquely identify its cause.

formulas.meaning: Mass divided by molar mass gives amount of a named substance.
symbols: n: amount in mol; m: sample mass in g; M: molar mass of that substance in g/mol.

formulas.meaning: V_m is gas volume per mole at the specified temperature and pressure.
symbols: V: gas volume in L; n: gas amount in mol; V_m: stated molar volume in L/mol.

simple.title: Mass versus gas reading
simple.given: A flask loses 0.440 g CO₂ only; M=44 g/mol and V_m=24 L/mol.
simple.find: Predict the collector volume if none is lost.
simple.problem: A flask loses 0.440 g CO₂ only; M=44 g/mol and V_m=24 L/mol. Predict the collector volume if none is lost.

challenge.title: Test a gas-removal model
challenge.given: Mass gain predicts 0.240±0.003 L removed, but the volume meter reads 0.300±0.010 L.
challenge.problem: Mass gain predicts 0.240±0.003 L removed, but the volume meter reads 0.300±0.010 L. Do the intervals agree?
steps: Prediction interval is 0.237–0.243 L.
Measurement interval is 0.290–0.310 L.
The intervals do not overlap.
challenge.answer: No; investigate additional effects or missing uncertainty

formula_cards.watch: A fitted value cannot also be independent validation. Hold conditions fixed when comparing trials.

learning_map.big_idea: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms. Balance the particle account first, then translate the equation into amounts and distinguish chemical change from collection or measurement loss.

basics.title: Atoms are rearranged, not created by ordinary reactions
basics.story: Reactants are starting substances; products are the substances formed. In an ordinary chemical reaction, each element’s atom count and total charge balance.
basics.why: In 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O, two hydrogen molecules react with one oxygen molecule to form two water molecules. Coefficients count entities or moles; they are not mass ratios.
basics.symbols: A closed material system retains all products, including gases, so its total mass is conserved.

basics.title: Amounts reveal the reaction ratio
basics.story: Convert measured masses to molar amounts before comparing a balanced equation. The limiting reactant is exhausted first under the stated complete-reaction model.
basics.why: For 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O, compare available H₂/2 and O₂/1. The smaller available reaction count limits how much water can form.
basics.symbols: n: amount (mol); m: mass (g); M: molar mass (g/mol). This conversion must use compatible mass units.

basics.title: Separate reaction energy from reaction speed
basics.story: Exothermic reactions transfer energy to surroundings; endothermic reactions absorb energy. Activation energy is a barrier on a reaction pathway.
basics.why: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation barrier. It changes rate without changing the energy difference between the same reactants and products.
basics.symbols: ΔH: reaction enthalpy change (often kJ/mol for the stated reaction basis); negative is exothermic under the stated convention.

routes.title: Use conservation and equation ratios
routes.cue: An equation, a particle diagram or a simple mass/amount is given.
routes.connection: Check the equation and material boundary before converting amounts.

routes.title: Track actual material through a process
routes.cue: The sample is impure, a gas is produced or collection is incomplete.
routes.connection: Use separate accounts for reactive content, chemical conversion and collected material.

routes.title: Distinguish chemical explanations
routes.cue: An energy profile or multiple measurements support competing mechanisms.
routes.connection: Separate the barrier from the net energy change; use independent checks to test the explanation.

learning_map.checkpoint: Can you show where every relevant atom goes and separate the theoretical product amount from the amount actually collected?

easy.context: Ice melts in one beaker; in another, vinegar and bicarbonate produce bubbles.
options: Both must be chemical because temperature changes
Melting is physical; bubbling supports a reaction but gas identity should be tested
Both are physical because atoms remain
Bubbles alone prove carbon dioxide
easy.hint: Separate a state change from evidence of new substances.
easy.feedback_correct: Correct. Bubbles alone do not establish that the gas is CO₂.
easy.feedback_incorrect: Conserving atoms does not make every change physical.
easy.explanation: Melting preserves water identity; bubbling in the reacting mixture is evidence that needs a gas test. Melting changes state only. Bubbling is reaction evidence, but identifying the gas strengthens the conclusion. Select Option 2: Melting is physical; bubbling supports a reaction but gas identity should be tested.

concept_discussion.given: A reaction in an open flask loses mass and then reaches a plateau. A student says all reactant must be consumed.
concept_discussion.prompt: Evaluate the inference and propose a discriminating test.
concept_discussion.discussion_points: Mass loss supports gas escape, but a plateau alone may reflect limiting-reactant exhaustion, equilibrium, leak behaviour or instrument resolution. Repeat in a closed gas-collection setup and vary each reactant amount; predicted final gas and leftover reactant distinguish explanations.

concept_discussion.given: A measured yield is 103%. The team argues the balanced equation is wrong.
concept_discussion.prompt: Evaluate and rank more likely explanations.
concept_discussion.discussion_points: A 103% yield more directly suggests retained solvent, contamination, wrong product composition or tare/calibration error than failure of atom conservation. Dry to constant mass, run a blank, verify product identity and repeat before revising the equation.

hard.title: Stretch 2: Distinguish mechanisms and apply new models
hard.description: Build a route from coupled constraints, identify the valid physical branch, and check the result. Work at your own pace; use the second session if needed.

concept_discussion.given: Two explanations fit a gas-volume plateau: reactant X is exhausted, or the reaction is reversible and reaches equilibrium.
concept_discussion.prompt: Design a test that distinguishes them.
concept_discussion.discussion_points: Adding X alone can restart production both when X was exhausted and when a reversible reaction was at equilibrium, so it is not a decisive test. Assay the remaining reactants independently with a sufficiently sensitive method and controlled temperature. Detectable X rules out complete X exhaustion but does not by itself prove equilibrium; where an equilibrium law is supplied, test the reaction quotient and compare responses to controlled perturbations. Check mixing and possible surface inhibition as alternative causes.

concept_discussion.given: A closed-system reaction loses 0.40 g according to the balance, while a duplicate gains 0.05 g. Both use the same nominal method.
concept_discussion.prompt: Evaluate the conservation claim and plan the next investigation.
concept_discussion.discussion_points: Opposite changes suggest apparatus or measurement faults rather than failure of conservation. Calibrate and tare the balance, run an unchanged-vessel blank, inspect seals, prevent external condensation or contamination, repeat and compare changes with uncertainty. A truly closed chemical system should retain total mass.

formula_cards.title: Acid/base particles and the pH scale
background: In water, H⁺ is shorthand for a solvated hydrogen ion, commonly represented as H₃O⁺. An acid donates a proton; a base accepts one. A soluble base is an alkali; its solution can supply OH⁻. Chloride Cl⁻ balances charge in hydrochloric acid solution.

Square brackets mean concentration of the named species in mol/L. log₁₀ asks which power of ten gives a number: log₁₀(10⁻⁴)=−4. A strong acid is extensively ionised; weak means partially ionised. Concentrated/dilute describes how much is dissolved per volume, a separate idea.

formulas.meaning: In the dilute ideal model, use the numerical H⁺ concentration in mol/L. pH has no unit.
symbols: [H⁺]: numerical hydrogen-ion concentration in mol/L; log₁₀: base-ten logarithm; pH has no unit.

formulas.meaning: A decrease of one pH unit corresponds to ten times the H⁺ concentration.
symbols: The numerical result is a concentration in mol/L; a more negative exponent gives a smaller concentration.

simple.title: Read a concentration
simple.problem: [H⁺]=1×10⁻⁴ mol/L. Find pH.
steps: The base-ten logarithm is −4.
pH is minus that value.

challenge.title: Compare two solutions
challenge.given: One solution is pH 2, another pH 5.
challenge.problem: One solution is pH 2, another pH 5. Find the H⁺ concentration ratio.
steps: Concentrations are 10⁻² and 10⁻⁵ mol/L.
Divide: 10⁻²/10⁻⁵=10³.
challenge.answer: The pH 2 solution has 1000 times greater [H⁺].

formula_cards.watch: Do not average pH values when mixing solutions; combine mole amounts first.

formula_cards.title: Concentration, aliquots and dilution
background: Molar concentration c is amount per litre of solution. The concentration unit M means mol/L; it does not mean mass or molar mass in this chapter. Convert mL to L by dividing by 1000.

An aliquot is a measured portion taken from a well-mixed solution. Adding solvent conserves solute amount in the transferred portion, but changes concentration and total volume. Diluted to 100 mL means final total volume 100 mL.

formulas.meaning: c is molar concentration in mol/L and V is solution volume in L.
symbols: n: solute amount in mol; c: concentration in mol/L (also called M); V: solution volume in L.

formulas.meaning: For the same dissolved substance, dilution conserves amount if none reacts or is lost.
symbols: c₁,c₂: before/after concentrations in matching units; V₁,V₂: transferred initial and final total volumes in matching units.

simple.title: One dilution
simple.given: 20 mL of 0.50 mol/L solution is diluted to 100 mL.
simple.problem: 20 mL of 0.50 mol/L solution is diluted to 100 mL. Find final concentration.
steps: Initial amount=0.50×0.020=0.010 mol.
Divide this same amount by final 0.100 L.

challenge.title: Serial transfer
challenge.given: 10 mL of 1.20 M is diluted to 200 mL; 25 mL of it is then diluted to 100 mL.
challenge.problem: 10 mL of 1.20 M is diluted to 200 mL; 25 mL of it is then diluted to 100 mL. Find final concentration.
steps: First concentration=1.20×10/200=0.060 M.
The aliquot has that concentration but only part of the batch’s solute.
Second concentration=0.060×25/100.

formula_cards.watch: The second aliquot is not the entire first dilution; track the amount transferred.

formula_cards.title: Neutralisation and titration
background: Neutralisation consumes H⁺ and OH⁻. Balance the acid/base equation before counting available ion amounts. H₂SO₄ supplies two acid equivalents in the complete-neutralisation model; Ca(OH)₂ supplies two OH⁻ per formula unit.

A titration uses a known-concentration titrant added to a measured aliquot until an endpoint signals near-equivalence. A pipette measures the aliquot; a burette delivers the difference of two position readings. Similar repeat titres are concordant; a rough trial locates the approximate endpoint.

formulas.meaning: Hydrogen and hydroxide ions react in a one-to-one amount ratio.
symbols: H⁺: hydrogen ion; OH⁻: hydroxide ion; H₂O: water. Superscripts ± denote charge, while the subscript 2 counts H atoms.

formulas.meaning: c is molar concentration in mol/L and V is solution volume in L.
symbols: n: solute amount in mol; c: concentration in mol/L (also called M); V: solution volume in L.

simple.title: One-to-one titration
simple.given: 25.0 mL of 0.200 M HCl fully neutralises NaOH.
simple.problem: 25.0 mL of 0.200 M HCl fully neutralises NaOH. Find NaOH amount.
steps: HCl+NaOH→NaCl+H₂O uses equal amounts.

challenge.title: Excess ions
challenge.given: 25 mL 0.100 M Ca(OH)₂ is mixed with 60 mL 0.100 M HCl.
challenge.problem: 25 mL 0.100 M Ca(OH)₂ is mixed with 60 mL 0.100 M HCl. Find excess [H⁺].
steps: H⁺ amount=0.060×0.100=0.006 mol; 0.001 mol remains.
Total volume is 0.085 L; divide the excess by this.

formula_cards.watch: A common additive burette offset cancels in a difference; a scale factor does not. Neutralisation does not always mean equal solution volumes.

figures.title: Titration quantities
figures.alt: Burette with known base over a flask containing a measured acid aliquot.
figures.caption: Original BEN Science schematic; use the stated data, not the drawing scale.

formula_cards.title: Rates, curves and collision conditions
background: Reacting particles must encounter one another in a suitable configuration with enough energy to pass an activation barrier. More exposed solid surface or higher reactant concentration can increase successful encounters.

A gas curve’s slope describes production rate. Its plateau describes total collected product. A tangent gives local instantaneous slope; a chord over an interval gives average slope. Temperature and catalyst can change rate without changing stoichiometric product amount.

formulas.meaning: Average gas-volume production rate is volume change divided by elapsed time.
symbols: ΔV: gas-volume increase in mL; Δt: elapsed time in s; this rate has unit mL/s.

formulas.meaning: For equal reaction extent and comparable rate behaviour, rate is inversely proportional to endpoint time.
symbols: r₁,r₂: average rates to the same endpoint; t₁,t₂: corresponding times in s. Only their dimensionless ratio is needed.

simple.title: Average rate
simple.given: 48 mL gas forms in 20 s.
simple.problem: 48 mL gas forms in 20 s. Find average rate.
steps: Volume change is 48−0=48 mL.
Time interval is 20−0=20 s.
Divide 48/20.

challenge.title: Fixed endpoint comparison
challenge.given: The same product amount is reached in 80 s and 50 s.
challenge.problem: The same product amount is reached in 80 s and 50 s. Compare average rates.
steps: Each rate is the same amount divided by its own time.
The amount cancels in their ratio.
New/old rate=80/50.

formula_cards.watch: A powder has more exposed surface, not more total atoms than equal-mass chips. Compare matched temperature, acid and collection conditions.

figures.title: Reading a rate curve
figures.alt: A rising gas volume curve with a tangent and a marked final plateau.
figures.caption: Original BEN Science schematic; use the stated data, not the drawing scale.

formula_cards.title: Empirical scaling and evidence
background: A rate law summarises measurements over a tested range. Do not obtain its concentration exponents directly from the balanced reaction coefficients. Isolate one changed concentration at a time.

An independent calibration can reveal systematic scale error even when repeated readings agree. A collector leak may scale both recorded slope and plateau; this does not necessarily change the reaction occurring in the flask.

formulas.meaning: An empirical initial-rate model: concentration exponents must be inferred from controlled trials.
symbols: [A],[B]: reactant concentrations in mol/L; m,n: fitted exponents, no unit; k: a constant whose unit depends on the chosen rate and exponents.

formulas.meaning: Conversion fraction compares current product with its complete-reaction amount.
symbols: x: reacted fraction, no unit; V: current gas volume; V_final: complete-reaction volume at the same conditions.

simple.title: Infer an exponent
simple.given: Doubling A with B fixed multiplies rate by four.
simple.find: Find the power of A in a power-law model.
simple.problem: Doubling A with B fixed multiplies rate by four. Find the power of A in a power-law model.
steps: Let rate be proportional to [A]^m.
The ratio gives 2^m=4.

challenge.title: Mixed concentration changes
challenge.given: Rate is proportional to [A]²[B]. A triples and B halves.
challenge.problem: Rate is proportional to [A]²[B]. A triples and B halves. Find rate factor.
steps: Square the A factor: 3²=9.
Multiply by B factor 0.5.

formula_cards.watch: A faster raw volume slope can reflect a larger final amount; normalise only under the stated kinetic and collection model.

learning_map.big_idea: Amount, concentration, acidity and speed answer different questions. Count reacting particles first, then ask how concentrated they are and how quickly the reaction changes the measurement.

basics.title: Acidity describes hydrogen-ion concentration
basics.story: In the introductory aqueous model, acids increase hydrogen-ion concentration and bases can accept hydrogen ions or provide hydroxide ions. Acid strength describes degree of ionisation; concentration describes amount per solution volume.
basics.why: A dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid can have different amounts and different hydrogen-ion concentrations. Strong and concentrated are separate descriptions.
basics.symbols: [H⁺]: hydrogen-ion concentration in mol/L, here interpreted relative to 1 mol/L in the logarithm; pH has no unit. One pH unit corresponds to a tenfold concentration change.

basics.title: Amount and concentration are linked by solution volume
basics.story: Molar concentration is dissolved amount per solution volume. An aliquot is a measured portion of a well-mixed solution.
basics.why: Diluting with water preserves dissolved amount if no reaction or loss occurs; concentration changes because the solution volume changes.
basics.symbols: n: amount (mol); c: molar concentration (mol/L); V: solution volume (L). Convert mL to L before using c in mol/L.

basics.title: Neutralisation follows the balanced reaction
basics.story: In the simple strong-acid/strong-base model, H⁺ and OH⁻ react to form water. Find what is consumed and what remains before calculating final concentration.
basics.why: Equal volumes need not contain equal reacting amounts. A balanced equation may require more than one mole of acid or base, so a 1:1 volume shortcut is unsafe.
basics.symbols: OH⁻: hydroxide ion. The coefficients in the actual balanced equation determine the mole ratio.

basics.title: Rate is a change per unit time
basics.story: On an amount–time or gas-volume–time graph, slope represents rate. The final height represents how much accumulated, which is a different quantity.
basics.why: A steeper early slope need not mean more final product. Concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts can alter effective collision conditions.
basics.symbols: ΔV: change in measured gas volume; Δt: elapsed time; average rate has the chosen volume/time unit. This gas V is distinct from the solution volume above.

routes.title: Separate the quantities
routes.cue: An acid is diluted, a portion is sampled or reactants are mixed.
routes.connection: Identify whether the question concerns pH, total amount, concentration or the neutralisation ratio.

routes.title: Read rate evidence
routes.cue: A time curve or a controlled comparison is given.
routes.connection: Use slopes for rate and plateaus for total amount; match all other experimental conditions.

routes.title: Infer an empirical model
routes.cue: Several runs suggest reaction orders or competing explanations.
routes.connection: Use a rate law only under its stated or inferred conditions; unknown powers are not automatically equation coefficients.

learning_map.checkpoint: Can you distinguish the amount present, hydrogen-ion concentration, total product and reaction rate before selecting a calculation?

test.given: A collector follows Q(t)=Q∞[1−exp(−k(t−τ))] after a fixed start delay τ; before that it reads 0. The constants Q∞,k,τ are unknown. Readings are Q(10 s)=20 mL,Q(20 s)=60 mL,Q(30 s)=80 mL. Assume the model is exact, k>0 and 0≤τ<10 s.
test.context: A collector follows Q(t)=Q∞[1−exp(−k(t−τ))] after a fixed start delay τ; before that it reads 0. The constants Q∞,k,τ are unknown. Readings are Q(10 s)=20 mL,Q(20 s)=60 mL,Q(30 s)=80 mL. Assume the model is exact, k>0 and 0≤τ<10 s.
test.find: Find τ.
test.prompt: Find τ.
test.hint: Use equal-time increments to infer the decay factor before finding the hidden plateau.
test.feedback_correct: Correct. The fitted plateau, rate and delay reproduce all three readings and satisfy the allowed start interval.
test.feedback_incorrect: A first nonzero reading does not locate the true reaction start; the delay must be inferred.
test.explanation: In equal 10 s intervals the increments are 40 and 20 mL. Their ratio is exp(−10k)=0.500, so k=ln 2/10. The remaining volume at 20 s is twice the next 20 mL increment, hence 40 mL; Q∞=60+40=100 mL. At 10 s, exp[−k(10−τ)]=0.800, giving τ=10+ln 0.800/k=6.78072 s.

concept_discussion.discussion_points: Both concentration and temperature can raise rate, so their effects are confounded. Hold temperature constant in a water bath, change only concentration, repeat trials and compare the same rate measure.

concept_discussion.discussion_points: Water droplets dilute the pipetted acid, so the fixed aliquot contains fewer moles and requires a smaller base titre. Treating it as undiluted makes the calculated acid concentration too low.

concept_discussion.given: Rate data from increasing acid concentration curve upward on a rate-versus-concentration plot. Temperature also rose by 3°C across the run order.
concept_discussion.prompt: Design an analysis and repeat plan that tests whether curvature is chemical or thermal drift.
concept_discussion.discussion_points: Thermal drift can imitate superlinear concentration dependence. Repeat in a controlled bath, randomise concentration order, use replicates and consistent initial-rate extraction. concept_discussion.given: Three acid–carbonate runs have equal carbonate moles. The hottest run is fastest but has the lowest collected gas plateau.
concept_discussion.prompt: Interpret the two observations and propose a check.
concept_discussion.discussion_points: Higher temperature plausibly raises rate, but equal carbonate amount should give equal theoretical CO₂. The lower plateau suggests collection loss, leakage, changed gas conditions or solubility effects. Use sealed injection, compare gas volumes at common temperature and pressure, leak-test and confirm with mass loss.

formula_cards.title: Density and the volume you measure
background: Density is mass per volume. For a composite, add masses and volumes before dividing. A simple average of densities works only for equal component volumes.

External volume includes pores. Solid-material volume excludes them. A sealed pore excludes water; an open pore may fill, changing displacement and absorbed-water measurements. Keep the volume definition attached to every density.

formulas.meaning: Bulk density uses external volume; material density excludes pores.
symbols: ρ: density; m: mass; V: explicitly defined sample volume. Common units: kg/m³ or g/cm³.

simple.problem: Mass=240 g; volume=80 cm³. Find density.

challenge.given: 100 cm³ of density 2 g/cm³ is joined to 50 cm³ of density 8 g/cm³ without extra gaps.
challenge.problem: 100 cm³ of density 2 g/cm³ is joined to 50 cm³ of density 8 g/cm³ without extra gaps. Find bulk density.
steps: Masses are 200 g and 400 g.

formula_cards.watch: Use 1 mL=1 cm³, 1 cm²=10⁻⁴ m² and 1 cm³=10⁻⁶ m³ when converting.

formula_cards.title: Pressure and connected resting liquids
background: Pressure is force normal to a surface per unit area. Absolute pressure includes atmospheric pressure; gauge pressure is measured relative to it.

A deeper surface supports more liquid above it, so pressure increases by ρg times vertical depth. Shape does not enter this relation. In connected, stationary liquid of one density, equal-height points have equal pressure.

formulas.meaning: Pressure is normal force per area; 1 Pa=1 N/m².
symbols: p: pressure in Pa; F_perp: normal force in N; A: loaded area in m².

formulas.meaning: Pressure increases downwards in a uniform resting liquid; Δh is vertical depth difference.
symbols: Δp: deeper minus shallower pressure in Pa; ρ: liquid density in kg/m³; g: m/s²; Δh: vertical depth increase in m.

simple.title: Depth pressure
simple.given: Water has ρ=1000 kg/m³, g=9.8 m/s² and depth 2.5 m below an open surface.
simple.problem: Water has ρ=1000 kg/m³, g=9.8 m/s² and depth 2.5 m below an open surface. Find gauge pressure.
steps: Gauge pressure at the surface is zero.

challenge.problem: Oil ρ=800 kg/m³ is 1.5 m deep over 2 m water ρ=1000 kg/m³; g=9.8 m/s². Find bottom gauge pressure.

formula_cards.watch: For hydraulics, compare piston pressures at equal height; add hydrostatic correction when heights differ.

formula_cards.title: Buoyancy, floating and cable directions
background: Fluid pushes harder on lower surfaces than upper ones. The net upward force equals the weight of displaced fluid. For a sealed, fully submerged body, displaced volume is its external volume.

A freely floating object adjusts its submerged volume until buoyancy equals weight. A cable can pull only along itself: a support above pulls up, while an anchor below pulls down. Draw the object’s forces before choosing the tension equation.

formulas.meaning: Net fluid pressure force equals the weight of liquid excluded by the object.
symbols: F_b: buoyancy in N; ρ_f: fluid density in kg/m³; g: m/s²; V_displaced: excluded fluid volume in m³.

formulas.meaning: Weight is gravitational force; mass and weight have different units.
symbols: W: weight in N; m: mass in kg; g: gravitational acceleration magnitude in m/s².

formulas.meaning: Use signed force components on a selected object; zero net force means zero acceleration.
symbols: ΣF: resultant force component in N; m: kg; a: signed acceleration component in m/s².

steps: Buoyancy=10 N upward; weight=6 N downward.
Tension must act down along the cable.
Balance 10−6−T=0.

formula_cards.title: Forces, friction and motion
background: Choose an object and a positive direction. Include only external forces on that object. Equal and opposite interaction forces act on different objects and do not cancel within one object’s free-body diagram.
On a floor, a tilted pull changes the normal force N. Static friction adjusts to prevent slip until its maximum μ_sN. For motion reversal, split the path at the time velocity becomes zero.

formulas.meaning: Use signed force components on a selected object; zero net force means zero acceleration.
symbols: ΣF: resultant force component in N; m: kg; a: signed acceleration component in m/s².

formulas.meaning: Static friction adjusts up to μ_sN; equality applies only at impending slip.
symbols: f_s: static friction magnitude in N; μ_s: static coefficient, no unit; N: normal contact force in N.

formulas.meaning: For constant acceleration along one chosen signed axis. s is displacement, not total path length.
symbols: u,v: initial/final signed velocities in m/s; a: constant acceleration in m/s²; t: s; s: displacement in m.

simple.title: Resultant force
simple.given: Mass=3 kg, acceleration=2.5 m/s² rightwards.
simple.problem: Mass=3 kg, acceleration=2.5 m/s² rightwards. Find resultant force.

challenge.title: Distance with reversal
challenge.given: Initial velocity is +4 m/s and acceleration −2 m/s² for 3 s.
challenge.problem: Initial velocity is +4 m/s and acceleration −2 m/s² for 3 s. Find total distance.
steps: The object stops at 2 s after moving 4 m right.
For the final second it moves 1 m left.
Add positive path lengths 4+1.

formula_cards.watch: At equilibrium N is not automatically mg: include vertical applied forces and buoyancy.

formula_cards.title: Work, energy and scaling
background: Net work changes kinetic energy. Constant opposing force removes a fixed energy per metre, which makes stopping distance proportional to initial speed squared.

For a proportional law, compare ratios while holding the model constants fixed. Square roots are needed when solving a squared quantity such as T². Only the physically meaningful positive period is retained.

formulas.meaning: Kinetic energy is non-negative and depends on speed squared.
symbols: K: kinetic energy in J; m: kg; v: speed in m/s.

formulas.meaning: Net work changes kinetic energy; for a constant force parallel to displacement, work=force×distance.
symbols: W_net: sum of external force work in J; ΔK: final minus initial kinetic energy in J.

formulas.meaning: For y proportional to xⁿ with unchanged proportionality constant.
symbols: x,y: quantities in the proportional relationship; subscripts label trials; exponent n has no unit.

simple.title: Speed factor
simple.given: y is proportional to x² and x triples.
simple.problem: y is proportional to x² and x triples. Find the change in y.
steps: Form y₂/y₁=(x₂/x₁)².
Insert 3².

challenge.title: Stopping distance
challenge.given: A cart stops in 1 m from 2 m/s under constant opposing force.
challenge.find: Predict distance from 4 m/s with the same mass and force.
challenge.problem: A cart stops in 1 m from 2 m/s under constant opposing force. Predict distance from 4 m/s with the same mass and force.
steps: Initial kinetic energy increases by (4/2)²=4.
The force removes the same energy per metre.
Stopping distance therefore increases fourfold.

formula_cards.watch: Energy uses speed squared; a negative velocity does not imply negative kinetic energy.

formula_cards.title: Algebra, graphs and model offsets
background: Apply the same operation to both sides of an equation. A second independent constraint lets you solve two unknowns. Keep units through each operation.

Gradient is vertical change divided by horizontal change. Signed area under a velocity–time graph is displacement. Linearisation means plotting transformed variables so a proposed curved relationship becomes a line; the intercept and residuals still matter.

formulas.meaning: A straight line has gradient k=Δy/Δx and intercept b; the axes set their units.
symbols: x: horizontal-axis quantity; y: vertical-axis quantity; k: gradient with units y/x; b: intercept with units y.

formulas.meaning: Ideal small-angle pendulum, length from pivot to bob centre; T is period.
symbols: T: oscillation period in s; L: pivot-to-bob-centre length in m; g: m/s²; π≈3.14159.

simple.title: Solve and substitute
simple.problem: 12=3x−6. Find x.
steps: Add 6 to both sides: 18=3x.
Divide both sides by 3: x=6.
Substitute 3×6−6=12.

challenge.title: Length offset from a line
challenge.given: Pendulum data give T²=4.00L_read+0.400, with T in s and lengths in m. Actual length is L_read+δ.
challenge.problem: Pendulum data give T²=4.00L_read+0.400, with T in s and lengths in m. Actual length is L_read+δ. Find δ.
steps: Write T²=4.00(L_read+δ).
Compare constant terms: 4.00δ=0.400.

formula_cards.watch: A graph’s axes define its gradient units. A nonzero intercept can be a real offset and is not automatically random error.

basics.title: Density and pressure refer to different comparisons
basics.story: Density is mass per volume. Pressure is normal force per area. Identify whether a stated volume includes holes and whether a pressure is absolute or a difference.
basics.why: For a resting liquid of constant density, pressure differences depend on vertical depth, not the shape of a connecting tube.
basics.symbols: ρ: density (kg/m³); m: mass (kg); V: volume (m³); Δp: pressure difference (Pa); g: gravitational acceleration (m/s²); Δh: vertical depth difference (m).

basics.title: Floating is a force balance
basics.story: Buoyancy comes from unequal fluid pressures across an object. Its magnitude equals the weight of displaced fluid under the stated static-fluid model.
basics.why: Use displaced fluid volume, not automatically total object volume. Include weight and any cable force before claiming buoyancy equals weight.
basics.symbols: F_b: buoyant force (N); ρ_f: fluid density (kg/m³); V_displaced: displaced volume (m³).

basics.title: Algebra should preserve the physical model
basics.story: A straight-line graph has a gradient and may have a nonzero intercept. Ratios cancel only factors that really stay fixed.
basics.why: Before rearranging, predict signs and limiting behaviour. If a fitted line has a nonzero intercept, a proportional relation through the origin cannot represent the entire measurement without an offset.
basics.symbols: In y=kx+b, k is gradient (y-unit/x-unit), b is intercept (y-unit). The symbol k has a different meaning in other chapters.

A solid is suspended by an external stand and fully immersed without touching the vessel; no water spills and the scale now reads 2.160 kg. Drain 0.100 kg water while keeping the solid immersed. test.given: A 2.00 kg sled starts from rest and is pulled 10.0 m by a 10.0 N rope 30° above horizontal. Its speed then is 6.00 m/s. The horizontal surface has one constant kinetic friction coefficient. The rope is removed immediately and the sled coasts to rest. Use g=10 m/s².
test.context: A 2.00 kg sled starts from rest and is pulled 10.0 m by a 10.0 N rope 30° above horizontal. Its speed then is 6.00 m/s. The horizontal surface has one constant kinetic friction coefficient. The rope is removed immediately and the sled coasts to rest. Use g=10 m/s².
test.find: Find the coasting distance after rope removal.
test.prompt: Find the coasting distance after rope removal.
test.hint: Infer friction from the first energy balance, then redraw forces for the coast.
test.feedback_correct: Correct. The pull reduced friction by lifting the sled; that reduction disappears during coasting.
test.feedback_incorrect: Using the pulling-stage friction force after the rope is removed ignores the changed normal load.
test.explanation: During pulling, the kinetic gain 36 J over 10 m gives net horizontal force 3.60 N. Normal force is 20−10sin 30°=15.0 N. Thus μ=(10cos 30°−3.60)/15=0.337350. After removal normal force becomes 20.0 N. Stopping requires 36 J=μ(20)d, giving d=5.33570 m.
