formula_cards.title: Gas pressure as a thermometer
background: Use the gas model from Week 1. P is absolute pressure, T is kelvin and n counts moles of all gas particles. In a sealed rigid system, n and V stay fixed, making P proportional to T.

A pressure change identifies temperature only when gas amount and volume are controlled. If a reaction adds particles, include the new n separately. Couple the inferred temperature rise to the appropriate heat capacity.

formulas.meaning: Absolute pressure P, absolute temperature T and gas amount n; choose consistent units for R.
symbols: P: absolute pressure; V: gas volume; n: mol; T: K. R=8.314 J/(mol K) for Pa and m³, or 8.314 kPa·L/(mol K) for kPa and L.

formulas.meaning: C is a total heat capacity in J/K; distinguish it from specific heat c.
symbols: Q: stored heat in J; C: total heat capacity in J/K; ΔT: temperature rise in K.

simple.title: Fixed vessel
simple.given: A sealed rigid ideal gas rises from 100 kPa at 300 K to 110 kPa.
simple.problem: A sealed rigid ideal gas rises from 100 kPa at 300 K to 110 kPa. Find final temperature.
steps: With n and V fixed, T₂/T₁=P₂/P₁.

challenge.title: Infer energy loss
challenge.given: The gas and vessel have C=100 J/K and receive 4000 J electrically during that change.
challenge.find: Find energy lost to the room.
challenge.problem: The gas and vessel have C=100 J/K and receive 4000 J electrically during that change. Find energy lost to the room.
steps: Stored energy=CΔT=100×30=3000 J.
Input=storage+loss, so loss=4000−3000.

formula_cards.watch: Changes in n, V and T multiply in P₂/P₁; do not attribute every pressure change to heating.

formula_cards.title: Electrical supply and thermal storage
background: Use the same component’s current and voltage for its power. A real cell’s emf includes energy later dissipated internally; terminal voltage is what reaches the external circuit.
For temperature change use heat capacity; at a melting plateau use latent heat. Efficiency applies at the specified boundary, after identifying which power and energy actually reach the sample.

formulas.meaning: Voltage V across a resistor in volts, current I through it in amperes, and resistance R in ohms.
symbols: V: component voltage in V; I: its current in A; R: component resistance in Ω.

formulas.meaning: Steady electrical power; the resistor form uses the voltage across that resistor.
symbols: P: W; V: voltage across this resistor in V; I: A; R: Ω.

formulas.meaning: A discharging cell loses Ir volts internally.
symbols: ε: emf in V; V: terminal voltage in V; I: discharge current in A; r: internal resistance in Ω.

formulas.meaning: Energy from constant power over the chosen interval.
symbols: E: transferred energy in J; P: constant power in W; t: duration in s.

formulas.meaning: For heating without a phase change; mc is sample heat capacity.
symbols: Q: J; m: kg; c: specific heat in J/(kg K); ΔT: temperature rise in K.

formulas.meaning: Melting ice at its melting temperature requires latent heat, not a temperature rise.
symbols: Q: energy in J; m: melted mass in kg; L_f: specific latent heat of fusion in J/kg.

formulas.meaning: Useful fraction of the input reaching the specified system.
symbols: η: useful fraction; Q_useful and E_input: energies in J for the same time interval.

simple.title: Useful energy
simple.given: A 100 W heater runs 180 s; 80% reaches the sample.
simple.problem: A 100 W heater runs 180 s; 80% reaches the sample. Find useful energy.
steps: Electrical energy=100×180=18000 J.
Useful energy=0.80×18000.

challenge.title: Battery-powered melting
challenge.given: ε=12 V, r=1 Ω, heater R=5 Ω; 80% of heater power reaches ice at 0°C for 100 s.
challenge.problem: ε=12 V, r=1 Ω, heater R=5 Ω; 80% of heater power reaches ice at 0°C for 100 s. Find useful melting energy.
steps: I=12/(1+5)=2 A; heater power=I²R=20 W.
Useful energy=0.80×20×100.

formula_cards.watch: C is J/K for the whole system; specific heat c is J/(kg K) for one material.

formula_cards.title: Wave and light routes
background: Use Week 3 wave relations and Week 4 ray models. Count whether the measured time is one-way or round-trip. A reflected pulse can provide the speed later used for a wavelength calculation.

For a string, the force actually transmitted to it is the tension; a submerged hanging load transmits apparent weight, not its air weight. For light transit use the path length inside each medium and the supplied speed index.

formulas.meaning: Wave speed, frequency and wavelength in the same medium.
symbols: v: wave speed in m/s; f: frequency in Hz; λ: wavelength in m.

formulas.meaning: Fixed-ended string fundamental; F_T is tension and μ is mass per unit length.
symbols: f₁: Hz; L: vibrating length in m; F_T: tension in N; μ: mass per unit length in kg/m.

formulas.meaning: Refraction angles to the normal; here n denotes refractive index, not gas amount.
symbols: 1,2 label the two media; n₁,n₂ are dimensionless indices; θ₁,θ₂ are angles to the boundary normal.

formulas.meaning: For the given transit-speed index n and path length d; c is vacuum light speed.
symbols: t: transit time in s; n: speed index; d: actual optical path length in m; c: vacuum speed in m/s.

simple.title: Echo to wavelength
simple.given: A pulse returns from a target 0.60 m away in 4 ms; continuous frequency is 1500 Hz.
simple.problem: A pulse returns from a target 0.60 m away in 4 ms; continuous frequency is 1500 Hz. Find wavelength.
steps: Round-trip path=1.20 m, so v=1.20/0.004=300 m/s.

challenge.title: Additional optical delay
challenge.given: A 0.30 m block has n=1.50 instead of an equal vacuum path.
challenge.problem: A 0.30 m block has n=1.50 instead of an equal vacuum path. Find one-way extra time.
steps: Block time=1.50×0.30/c=1.50 ns.
Vacuum time=0.30/c=1.00 ns.
Subtract the baseline transit.

formula_cards.watch: A transit-time difference compares equal geometrical paths. A reflected pulse traverses the material twice.

formula_cards.title: Chemical amounts and electrical measurements
background: Use balanced reaction ratios from Reactions and amount accounting from Acids. A product count follows its stoichiometric relation, not the charge number or formula subscript taken in isolation.

Electrolysis is chemical change driven by current: a positive copper ion gains electrons to become neutral Cu. A conductivity instrument instead measures current through a solution. In the stated idealised sensor model I=kc_sV_e, more ions per volume or higher voltage gives a larger current; k is fixed only for the same sensor and solution type.

formulas.meaning: Molar amount from solution concentration c_s and solution volume V_s.
symbols: n: solute amount in mol; c_s: concentration in mol/L; V_s: solution volume in L.

formulas.meaning: Conserved solute during transfer and dilution with no reaction or loss.
symbols: c₁,c₂: concentrations; V_s,1,V_s,2: initial and final solution volumes, using matching units.

formulas.meaning: Electron count from charge magnitude Q_e and elementary-charge magnitude e.
symbols: N_e: number of electrons; Q_e: total charge magnitude in C; e: one electron’s charge magnitude, about 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C.

formulas.meaning: Supplied idealised conductivity model; c_s is concentration, V_e applied voltage and k a fixed sensor constant.
symbols: I: A; c_s: mol/L; V_e: electrical voltage in V; k: fixed sensor coefficient in A·L/(mol·V) for these units.

simple.title: Electron-to-atom count
simple.given: Cu²⁺+2e⁻→Cu; 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ C of electron charge is delivered with e=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C.
simple.problem: Cu²⁺+2e⁻→Cu; 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ C of electron charge is delivered with e=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C. Count deposited Cu atoms.
steps: Electron count=Q/e=2.
Each Cu²⁺ requires two electrons.

challenge.title: Inverse conductivity comparison
challenge.given: Under I=kc_sV_e, a diluted solution carries 0.6 times current at 1.5 times voltage.
challenge.problem: Under I=kc_sV_e, a diluted solution carries 0.6 times current at 1.5 times voltage. Find concentration and solution-volume factors.
steps: Conserved solute gives V_s,new/V_s,old=1/0.4.

formula_cards.watch: V_e is electrical potential while V_s is solution volume; use explicit subscripts to avoid confusing the two meanings of V.

formula_cards.title: Buoyancy, momentum and work
background: Use the diagnostic chapter’s force balance and Mechanics conservation laws. Buoyancy changes support tension but does not alter an object’s mass.

In a sticking collision conserve momentum over the short impact if external impulse is negligible. Kinetic energy is not conserved during sticking. After impact, the lost motion energy can be accounted for as heat if the problem explicitly identifies where it goes.

formulas.meaning: Use the stated material, external or displaced volume.
symbols: ρ: density; m: mass; V: explicitly defined sample volume. Common units: kg/m³ or g/cm³.

formulas.meaning: Fluid pressure provides buoyancy equal to displaced-fluid weight.
symbols: F_b: buoyancy in N; ρ_f: fluid density in kg/m³; g: m/s²; V_displaced: excluded fluid volume in m³.

formulas.meaning: Momentum is conserved when external impulse is negligible; use signed velocities.
symbols: i labels bodies; mᵢ: kg; uᵢ,vᵢ: signed before/after velocities in m/s.

formulas.meaning: Motion energy uses speed squared.
symbols: K: kinetic energy in J; m: kg; v: speed in m/s.

formulas.meaning: Net work changes kinetic energy; constant parallel force does work Fd.
symbols: W_net: sum of external force work in J; ΔK: final minus initial kinetic energy in J.

simple.title: Submerged lift
simple.given: A 2 kg object of volume 0.001 m³ rises slowly through 0.50 m of water; ρ=1000 kg/m³, g=10 m/s²; ignore drag.
simple.problem: A 2 kg object of volume 0.001 m³ rises slowly through 0.50 m of water; ρ=1000 kg/m³, g=10 m/s²; ignore drag. Find cable work.
steps: Weight=20 N and buoyancy=10 N.
Constant speed requires tension 10 N.
Cable work=10×0.50.

challenge.title: Collision heat
challenge.given: A 1 kg cart at 4 m/s sticks to an identical resting cart. All lost motion energy heats a pad of heat capacity 20 J/K.
challenge.problem: A 1 kg cart at 4 m/s sticks to an identical resting cart. All lost motion energy heats a pad of heat capacity 20 J/K. Find temperature rise.
steps: Momentum gives final speed 2 m/s.
Kinetic energy falls from 8 J to 4 J.

formula_cards.watch: Select conservation law separately for each stage. Momentum conservation does not imply kinetic-energy conservation.

formula_cards.title: Graphs, scaling and independent evidence
background: Translate every axis, coefficient and fraction into a physical quantity before combining models. An inverse problem often needs two independent constraints to separate two unknowns.

Repeatability concerns scatter. Two apparently independent methods can still share a biased pipette, thermometer or starting sample. A validation check must avoid that shared source. Match a formula to its physical system and units, not merely to a familiar letter.

formulas.meaning: Resting liquid pressure rise with vertical depth.
symbols: Δp: deeper minus shallower pressure in Pa; ρ: liquid density in kg/m³; g: m/s²; Δh: vertical depth increase in m.

formulas.meaning: Conserved solute during transfer and dilution with no reaction or loss.
symbols: c₁,c₂: concentrations; V_s,1,V_s,2: initial and final solution volumes, using matching units.

simple.title: Remove pressure offset
simple.given: Lower and upper sensors read 17.0 and 14.6 kPa, separated by 0.30 m; g=10 m/s².
simple.problem: Lower and upper sensors read 17.0 and 14.6 kPa, separated by 0.30 m; g=10 m/s². Find liquid density.
steps: Pressure difference=2400 Pa.

challenge.title: Separate self-heating from bath warming
challenge.given: A resistor thermometer rises with probe voltage but a fixed-volume gas thermometer stays constant.
challenge.problem: A resistor thermometer rises with probe voltage but a fixed-volume gas thermometer stays constant. Choose a discriminating check.
steps: Hold the bath fixed while lowering probe power.
Measure resistance with negligible power and compare gas pressure again.
A changed resistor indication without changed gas pressure supports local self-heating.

learning_map.big_idea: An unfamiliar problem often links two familiar accounts through one shared quantity. Identify that shared quantity and carry its meaning and units across the boundary between models.
chain: Pass a consistent value between them

basics.title: Conservation links processes
basics.story: Mass, charge or energy leaving one part may enter another. State the system and the transfer before equating quantities.
basics.why: A heater’s electrical input and a sample’s thermal gain match only after accounting for other stores and losses. Conservation does not mean every measured energy is useful.

basics.title: A shared variable must keep its meaning
basics.story: Pressure may link a gas to a liquid column; temperature may link a thermometer to a thermal store; concentration may link chemistry to a sensor.
basics.why: List the units and state conditions on both sides. In this review, sensor-specific relations are supplied where first used; they are not general laws for every instrument.

basics.title: Evidence separates explanations
basics.story: One observation may fit several parameter combinations. Look for an independent measurement or a controlled change with a different predicted outcome.
basics.why: A good model predicts a new condition; merely fitting one data point does not establish a unique cause.

routes.title: Reconnect state and energy
routes.cue: A gas sensor or electrical supply is used in a thermal process.
routes.connection: Identify the shared temperature, power or energy, then include constraints and losses.

routes.title: Translate across a measuring system
routes.cue: Optical, chemical or electrical data measure a different underlying quantity.
routes.connection: Separate the physical process from the sensor or path model.

routes.title: Combine balances and challenge the model
routes.cue: Fluid forces, collisions, work or graph offsets interact.
routes.connection: Apply each conservation law only to the system and time interval for which its conditions hold.

learning_map.checkpoint: Can you explain what passes from one model to the next, with its units, and give an independent check of the combined result?

easy.given: A sealed gas is kept at fixed volume and amount. Temperature readings are 300,330,360 K and the corresponding absolute pressures are 100,110,126 kPa. Treat the first two readings as an exact calibration with no pressure offset.
easy.context: A sealed gas is kept at fixed volume and amount. Temperature readings are 300,330,360 K and the corresponding absolute pressures are 100,110,126 kPa. Treat the first two readings as an exact calibration with no pressure offset.
easy.find: Find how many kPa the third pressure exceeds the ideal-gas prediction.
easy.prompt: Find how many kPa the third pressure exceeds the ideal-gas prediction.
easy.hint: Use the calibration readings as a prediction, not as three numbers to average.
easy.feedback_correct: Correct. The requested residual diagnoses the observation rather than repeating a two-state substitution.

formula_cards.title: Classification and evolutionary relationships
background: Classification groups organisms by shared characteristics and ancestry. The naming hierarchy runs kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. A scientific species name combines genus and species. A dichotomous key uses two alternative descriptions at each step; follow observed traits rather than guessing a familiar name.

Bacteria are cellular organisms without a membrane-bound nucleus. Animals, plants and fungi have cells with nuclei; fungi obtain nutrients by absorption and do not photosynthesise. Viruses require host cells to reproduce. Many microorganisms are beneficial; not every microbe causes disease.

A phylogenetic tree represents inferred ancestry. A node represents a common ancestor; the branching pattern, not how close the printed tips lie, determines relatedness. A character may evolve independently in separate lineages. A tree is evidence-based and can change with new data.

A derived state is a character different from the inferred ancestral state, established here using a stated reference. Shared inherited states across independent markers can support shared ancestry; one similar colour can arise independently (convergence).

formula_cards.title: Cells, structures and scale
background: A cell membrane regulates exchange with the surroundings. Cytoplasm supports many reactions; a nucleus contains most DNA in typical plant and animal cells. Ribosomes assemble proteins. Mitochondria support aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in photosynthetic plant cells; not every plant cell has chloroplasts.

DNA stores sequence information. A gene is a DNA region whose product can contribute to a trait. Ribosomes make proteins; the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a membrane network involved in making and moving proteins and lipids. Mitochondria release usable energy in respiration; a cell does not obtain its energy merely by having a nucleus.

Plant cells usually have a cellulose wall and a large vacuole. Animal cells lack a cellulose wall. Bacteria have no membrane-bound nucleus. A tissue is a coordinated group of cells; an organ contains tissues; organ systems coordinate organs.

Magnification M=image size/actual size when the two lengths use the same unit. Resolution is the ability to distinguish nearby features; increasing display size alone cannot reveal information absent from the original image. One mm is 1000 μm.

A specialised cell has structures suited to a task: a root hair increases exchange area, while a red blood cell carries oxygen. A thin exchange barrier and maintained concentration difference help diffusion; simply making an image larger does not improve exchange or microscope resolution.

formula_cards.title: Membranes, diffusion and osmosis
background: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient through random motion. Net movement can stop at equilibrium while particles continue moving in both directions. Membrane permeability determines which substances can cross.

Concentration means amount per volume: c = n/V. Here n is amount of dissolved particles in mol, V is solution volume in L, and c has unit mol/L, also written M. One mol contains 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified particles. For the non-dissociating solutes in these tasks, 0.20 M means 0.20 mol of particles per litre. Solute amount is conserved when only water crosses, even though concentration changes.

Osmosis is net water movement through a selectively permeable membrane towards lower water potential. For the simple equal-pressure dilute solutions used here, that is towards the higher effective concentration of solute particles that cannot cross. Explicitly permeant solutes can change the final outcome.

Active transport can move substances against their concentration gradient using metabolic energy. Surface area grows with length squared while volume grows with length cubed; larger geometrically similar cells have less area per unit volume. Exchange also depends on membrane thickness and gradient.

Water potential describes the tendency of water to move: pressure raises it and dissolved particles lower it in this model. Compare both sides at the stated pressure. A flexible, unstretched bag can be treated as having negligible pressure difference; a stretched membrane or rigid cell wall can oppose further water entry. At equilibrium equal effective concentrations follow only under the stated equal-pressure conditions.

symbols: S: area; V: volume; a: cube side in matching units.

formula_cards.title: Nutrition, transport and gas exchange
background: Digestion breaks food into absorbable molecules. Carbohydrates and fats can supply energy; proteins supply amino acids for building and other functions. Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts. Absorption transfers nutrients across an exchange surface into transport systems.

An enzyme is a biological catalyst: it speeds a reaction without being used up overall. A substrate is the molecule it acts on; products are made. The active site is the binding/reaction region. In digestion, enzymes help break large food molecules into absorbable molecules. Temperature and pH can change activity; excessive heat can disrupt protein shape (denaturation). Low activity in the cold alone does not show permanent damage: test again at a common temperature. Rate means product amount divided by time. One μmol (micromole) is 10⁻⁶ mol; μmol/min measures the amount produced per minute. A blank lacks the biological component being tested but keeps the other measurement conditions; subtract its contribution.

In humans, lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide with blood. The heart drives circulation; haemoglobin in red cells carries much of the oxygen. Tissues consume oxygen during aerobic respiration. Thin moist surfaces and flow maintain exchange gradients. Kidneys help regulate water and dissolved substances and remove metabolic wastes.

Plants take up water and minerals through roots. Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals; phloem transports dissolved sugars between sources and sinks. Transpiration is water loss, mainly through leaf stomata. Closing stomata can reduce water loss and also limit carbon dioxide supply.

simple.title: Track oxygen
simple.given: Blood enters a resting tissue oxygen-rich and leaves with less oxygen.
steps: Oxygen moves towards consuming cells.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen.
The blood then carries a lower oxygen content away.

challenge.title: Separate temperature from lasting damage
challenge.given: Equal enzyme samples are pretreated at 5°C or 85°C, then both assayed at 30°C with fresh excess substrate. The cold-pretreated sample recovers activity; the heated sample remains low. An untreated sample is active.
steps: The final assay temperature is matched, so cold collisions during the assay cannot explain the difference.
Recovery after cold pretreatment shows that low activity in the cold need not be permanent.
Persistently low activity after heating supports heat-induced loss of function; shape damage is a mechanism consistent with the model, not directly imaged by the assay.
challenge.answer: Heating caused a lasting loss of measured activity under these conditions.

formula_cards.watch: Ventilation moves air; gas exchange crosses a surface; respiration is a cellular chemical process.

formula_cards.title: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration
background: Photosynthesis stores incoming light energy in organic matter: carbon dioxide plus water can form glucose and oxygen. Aerobic respiration transfers energy from organic molecules for cellular processes and releases carbon dioxide and water. Plants respire as well as photosynthesise.

In a simple oxygen measurement, net oxygen change=photosynthetic oxygen production−respiratory consumption, after correcting blanks. In darkness photosynthesis stops but respiration continues. Gross photosynthesis can be inferred by adding the separately justified respiration rate to the net light rate; assume the rate is unchanged only when stated.

Photosynthesis can be limited by light, carbon dioxide, temperature or other factors. A response plateau supports a limiting-factor hypothesis but does not identify the cause without a controlled intervention.

formulas.meaning: Rates must describe the same measured substance and time unit.
symbols: P_net: net production rate; P_gross: gross production; R: consumption rate.

formula_cards.watch: A net gas reading combines production, consumption and possible non-biological exchange.

formula_cards.title: Homeostasis, nerves and defence
background: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within a functional range. In negative feedback, a sensor detects a deviation, a control system changes effectors, and the response reduces the original deviation. A maintained steady value need not mean that no energy is used.

Nervous signals coordinate relatively rapid responses; hormones are chemical signals carried to responsive targets. After a rise in blood glucose, insulin normally promotes processes that lower it. Thermoregulation can change sweating, skin blood flow and muscle activity; the exact response depends on conditions.

Pathogens can cause disease. Physical barriers and immune responses protect the body. Vaccination prepares specific immune memory and can improve later responses. Antibiotics act on susceptible bacteria, not on viruses. Resistance can spread when heritable resistant variants survive treatment and reproduce.

In a feedback loop a receptor/sensor detects a change, a control centre coordinates a response, and an effector changes the regulated variable. For high blood glucose, insulin helps promote uptake/storage; when glucose falls, glucagon helps raise it. A reflex arc is a rapid sensory-neuron → central relay → motor-neuron → effector pathway; some responses occur before conscious awareness.

An antigen is a molecular feature recognised by the immune system. Some activated B cells produce antibodies that bind particular antigens; memory cells can persist. A later encounter with the same antigen can produce a faster, stronger response. Specificity matters: prior exposure to antigen X does not establish protection against an unrelated antigen Y. Compare matched groups and baseline antibody levels before attributing a response to memory.

For this glucose loop, pancreatic cells sense blood glucose: beta cells release insulin when glucose is high, while alpha cells release glucagon when glucose is low. Liver, muscle and other target tissues contribute to changing glucose storage, uptake or release. The diagram isolates the high-glucose branch, not every physiological pathway.

steps: The response opposes the initial rise.
It can bring temperature towards the range.

formula_cards.title: DNA, inheritance and reproduction
background: DNA carries genetic information. A gene is a DNA region contributing to a product or function; alleles are variants of a gene. Chromosomes contain DNA and many genes. A diploid cell has two chromosome sets; a haploid gamete has one. Mitosis normally maintains chromosome number; meiosis forms haploid products, and fertilisation combines two haploid sets.

Sexual reproduction combines genetic contributions and increases combinations of alleles. Asexual reproduction can produce genetically similar offspring, with mutation still possible. DNA replication copies genetic material before division; counting DNA molecules and counting chromosomes are different tasks.

For a stated single-gene complete-dominance model, Aa has the dominant phenotype and aa the recessive phenotype. A heterozygote Aa passes A or a with equal probability. Use the given segregation/independence assumptions; many real traits involve several genes and environment.

A Punnett square lists combinations of one gamete from each parent. Genotype is the allele combination; phenotype is the observable trait. A pedigree tracks a trait through a family; a labelled affected/unaffected pattern alone does not identify a unique inheritance model without assumptions. A carrier has a recessive allele without the recessive phenotype in the stated model.

Autosomal means located on a chromosome other than a sex chromosome. The single-gene crosses here assume the stated locus, segregation and phenotype rule; real traits may involve many genes and environmental influences.

formula_cards.title: Reproduction and development
background: Sexual reproduction combines haploid gametes at fertilisation to form a diploid zygote. Subsequent mitosis and differentiation support an embryo and specialised tissues. Asexual reproduction uses one parent without gamete fusion; offspring can still vary through mutation.

In flowering plants, anthers produce pollen; pollen transfer to a stigma is pollination. A pollen tube can deliver a male gamete to an ovule, where fertilisation can occur. After fertilisation an ovule can develop into a seed and the ovary into fruit. Pollination and fertilisation are different stages; failure at either can limit seed production.

In animals, testes and ovaries produce gametes, and reproductive hormones coordinate development and reproductive processes. Fertilisation and embryo development vary among species. Inheritance depends on gametes; parental care and environmental conditions can separately affect offspring survival.

formula_cards.watch: A successful early stage does not guarantee a successful final product.

formula_cards.title: Evolution, populations and ecosystems
background: Natural selection changes populations when heritable variants differ in survival or reproduction. Mutation supplies variation without anticipating need. Evidence for relatedness includes inherited molecular features and fossils; one shared appearance can be misleading.

Food-web arrows point from resource to consumer, following matter and energy transfer. Producers build organic matter; consumers obtain it from other organisms; decomposers recycle matter. Energy enters and leaves the system and is dissipated as heat; matter can cycle. Transfer efficiency must be given or inferred; it is not universally 10%.

Population change equals births plus immigration minus deaths and emigration over the same period. Competition, predation, disease and environmental change can alter these terms. A correlation does not identify the causal route.

A simple mark–recapture estimate is N≈MC/R: M animals are initially marked, C are caught in a later mixed sample and R of these are marked. It assumes a closed, well-mixed population, retained harmless marks and equal capture probabilities. Test those assumptions before trusting the estimate.

formulas.meaning: A simple closed-population mark–recapture estimate.
symbols: N: population estimate; M: initially marked; C: later catch; R: marked recaptures.

learning_map.big_idea: Explain a biological outcome through a mechanism: structures enable transport and reactions, information guides inheritance and regulation, and populations interact through limited resources.

basics.title: Cells are functioning systems with specialised structures
basics.story: A cell membrane controls exchanges; cytoplasm supports many reactions; genetic material carries information. Structure matters because it enables a process at a particular scale.
basics.why: An image can reveal shape or location, but a function claim needs evidence. Magnification changes image size, not the real object size.
basics.symbols: In M=I/A, M is magnification (no unit), I is image length and A is actual length. Use the same length unit before dividing.

basics.title: Transport follows gradients and membrane properties
basics.story: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient due to random motion. Osmosis is net water movement across a selectively permeable membrane towards lower water potential.
basics.why: For simple solutions under comparable pressure, an effectively non-penetrating solute lowers water potential. Which particles can cross the membrane determines the outcome. Smaller cells often exchange more efficiently because their surface area is large relative to volume.
basics.symbols: Selective permeability: some substances cross more easily than others. A gradient is a difference over distance.

basics.title: Matter cycles while energy is transferred
basics.story: Photosynthesis uses light energy to build organic molecules from carbon dioxide and water. Cellular respiration releases usable energy from chemical stores; plants respire as well as photosynthesise.
basics.why: Growth and gas exchange depend on gross production and respiration. Feeding relationships transfer matter and energy; energy is progressively dissipated rather than endlessly recycled.

basics.title: Genetic information and regulation affect outcomes
basics.story: DNA carries hereditary information; a gene is a DNA region contributing to a functional product. Alleles are versions of a gene. Regulation and feedback connect sensed changes to responses.
basics.why: An inheritance ratio requires a stated model of alleles, gametes and parent genotypes. A dominant allele need not be common, beneficial or a guarantee against environmental effects.

basics.title: Populations change through interacting causes
basics.story: Birth, death, migration, resource limits and interactions change population size. Natural selection changes inherited variation across generations when it affects survival or reproduction.
basics.why: A population estimate or association is bounded by its sampling and control assumptions. A single organism does not evolve because it “needs” to adapt.

routes.title: Connect structure to function
routes.cue: Classification, cells, transport and energy transformations are described.
routes.connection: Use observable features and the mechanism, then distinguish evidence from an unsupported function claim.

routes.title: Connect information to a response
routes.cue: A body regulates conditions or offspring inherit variants.
routes.connection: State the feedback or inheritance assumptions before predicting outcomes.

routes.title: Combine organisms and population evidence
routes.cue: Sampling, competition or environmental change enters.
routes.connection: Keep population mechanisms separate from the limitations of the evidence and sampling model.

learning_map.checkpoint: Can you give a mechanism for the result and identify the control or observation that would distinguish it from a competing explanation?

prerequisites: Reading axes, tables and controlled comparisons

introduction.title: How to study
introduction.body: Read the core model once. Use Foundation to check vocabulary and relationships, Core to connect evidence, and Stretch to compare explanations. Sample Test is an independent first attempt.

introduction.title: Data and scope
introduction.body: Question measurements are invented teaching data under the stated models. This is an introductory JSO breadth stage; independent full-paper performance and practical skills need separate assessment.

introduction.title: Reading and evidence
introduction.body: Use the 70-minute brief allowance in sections before the first relevant practice; it is a planning target, not measured learner time. Surface mixtures and tracer rules are explained at their first Core task. Measurements and examples are invented teaching data. This introduction does not replace map/rock identification, field measurements, practical skills or an unseen full-paper assessment.

mastery_targets.body: Connect rotation, tilt, lunar alignment and surface energy, distinguishing local flux from whole-planet averages.

mastery_targets.body: Conserve carbon and tracer inventories; distinguish stock, flux, forcing, feedback, warming rate and equilibrium.

formula_cards.title: Earth, Sun and Moon: geometry before names
background: Earth rotates approximately once per day, producing the day/night cycle. Its orbit around the Sun and tilted rotation axis produce seasonal changes in daylight and solar angle. The two hemispheres have opposite seasons. The main seasonal mechanism is axial tilt, not a large annual distance change.

The Moon reflects sunlight. Lunar phases result from viewing different portions of its sunlit half. A solar eclipse requires the Moon between Earth and Sun with suitable alignment; a lunar eclipse requires Earth between Sun and Moon. The tilted lunar orbit means alignment does not occur every month.

Tides arise from differences in gravitational acceleration across Earth, mainly from the Moon with a solar contribution. Alignment near new/full moon tends to give a larger tidal range (spring tides); near quarter phases the range is smaller (neap tides). Local coastlines and water dynamics affect actual tide times and heights.

An axis is the imaginary line Earth spins around; its tilt is about 23.5° from the perpendicular to its orbital plane. Higher solar elevation concentrates the same beam onto less horizontal area, while longer daylight extends energy input. A surface daylight-mean flux already refers to the stated surface: integrate it over that daylight, without dividing by four again. The factor four applies to the whole-sphere average of sunlight intercepted by a disk.

Tidal range means high-water level minus low-water level, in metres. Spring tide names the larger-range alignment pattern, not the season spring. Quadrature means the Sun and Moon directions are about 90° apart as viewed from Earth. It reduces their combined tide-raising pattern; it does not remove gravity or all tides. An ordinary lunar phase is an illumination/viewing effect; Earth’s shadow is needed only for a lunar eclipse.

simple.title: Opposite seasons
simple.given: The northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun.
steps: The north receives a higher solar angle and generally longer daylight.
The south is tilted away.
Northern summer and southern winter occur together.

challenge.title: Phase versus eclipse
challenge.given: A full moon occurs without an eclipse.
steps: A full phase means the visible lunar face is largely sunlit.
Earth’s shadow need not intersect the Moon.
The inclined lunar orbit permits a full moon above or below the shadow.
challenge.answer: Full phase does not guarantee shadow alignment.

formula_cards.watch: A phase describes illumination as seen from Earth; an eclipse requires a shadow alignment.

formula_cards.title: Plate motion and geological evidence
background: A tectonic plate is a relatively rigid piece of lithosphere: crust plus the uppermost mantle. The hotter mantle below can deform slowly while remaining mostly solid; it is not a global ocean of liquid magma. A reference frame states what motion is measured relative to, such as the ridge or a fixed mantle marker. Plates and the ridge itself can move in different frames.

At divergent boundaries plates move apart and new crust can form. At convergent boundaries plates approach; subduction can carry oceanic lithosphere down, while continent collisions can thicken crust. Transform boundaries mainly slide past. Earthquakes can occur at several boundary types; one event is insufficient to identify a boundary.

Evidence for plate motion includes matching geological/fossil patterns across separated continents, young seafloor at spreading ridges with older crust away, and paired magnetic reversal patterns. Interpret ages, distances and directions together.

For steady motion, distance=speed×time. A full separation rate between two plates differs from one-side spreading speed. One cm/yr equals 10 km per million years; always state which distance is measured.

As basalt cools, magnetic minerals can retain a record of Earth’s magnetic polarity. A reversal switches the polarity direction. Correlating the same dated reversal on both sides identifies crust formed at the same time. Equal-aged offsets add to the full separation since formation even if the ridge moved, provided the plates did not later deform and the markers are correctly matched.

formulas.meaning: Use a consistent reference and matching units.
symbols: d: distance travelled relative to the stated reference; v: corresponding constant speed; t: elapsed time. Use km/Myr or convert consistently. Myr is a duration of one million years; Ma denotes an age in millions of years before the present.

simple.title: One side
simple.given: Crust moves 20 km from a ridge in 1.0 million years.
steps: Speed=20 km per million years.
10 km per million years is 1 cm/yr.
Speed=2 cm/yr.

challenge.title: Both sides
challenge.given: Each side spreads away from a fixed ridge at 2 cm/yr.
challenge.find: Find full separation after 3 million years.
steps: Relative separation speed is 4 cm/yr.
This is 40 km per million years.
Over 3 million years separation is 120 km.

formula_cards.watch: Do not use the two-side separation rate for a one-side distance.

formula_cards.title: Rocks, minerals and relative time
background: A mineral has a characteristic composition and structure; a rock is an aggregate of minerals or other geological material. Igneous rock forms from cooling melt; slow cooling often permits larger crystals. Sedimentary rock forms through deposition and lithification, or chemical/biological accumulation. Metamorphism changes existing rock under heat, pressure and fluids without complete melting.

Weathering breaks down or alters material; erosion transports it; deposition places it. Burial, heating, uplift and melting connect the rock cycle. Melting followed by solidification gives an igneous path, not merely metamorphism.

In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, lower layers are generally older. A feature cutting another is younger than what it cuts. Included fragments are older than the rock containing them. An unconformity records erosion or missing deposition; thickness alone need not equal duration.

A dyke is sheet-like igneous rock formed when magma enters a fracture and solidifies. An intrusion is igneous material emplaced within older rock. A radiometric age of an intrusion mineral dates the stated crystallisation/closure event, not automatically the deposition of every nearby sediment. Larger Ma values mean further back in time. Slow versus fast cooling affects texture; pores and interlocking crystals can affect permeability and strength, but suitability for a use also needs actual property measurements.

simple.title: Cooling history
simple.given: Two samples have the same magma composition; one cools more slowly and forms larger crystals.
steps: Crystals grow while melt cools.
More growth time can permit larger crystals.
Composition alone does not determine crystal size.
simple.answer: Growth time is part of the explanation.

challenge.title: Order events
challenge.given: Undisturbed A lies below B. A dyke cuts both; an exposed erosion surface truncates the dyke and both layers. C was then deposited on that surface.
steps: A and B formed before the cutting dyke.
C was deposited after the dyke was truncated or covered.
Within undisturbed A/B, the lower layer is older.

formula_cards.watch: A missing layer can reflect erosion or non-deposition; it does not establish one exact duration.

formula_cards.title: Earth-system reservoirs and the carbon cycle
background: The atmosphere is the air, hydrosphere the water, biosphere living systems, and geosphere rocks and solid Earth. Carbon can be stored in air, dissolved water, organic matter, sediments and rocks. Photosynthesis transfers carbon into organic matter; respiration and combustion return it to other reservoirs. Weathering, burial and volcanism link slower rock pathways. Matter is conserved within the defined system even while it moves between reservoirs.

A reservoir stock is an amount, such as gigatonnes of carbon (Gt C). A flux is an amount per time, such as Gt C/year. Reservoir change=inflow−outflow over one interval. An equal gross exchange in each direction can produce zero net change while both fluxes remain large.

Carbon and carbon dioxide masses differ. CO₂ contains 12 mass units of carbon per 44 mass units of CO₂. Convert only when the reported units require it. A source/sink judgement must state the reservoir and interval.

Gt C means gigatonnes of carbon: 1 Gt = 10⁹ tonnes and 1 tonne = 1000 kg. Gt CO₂ instead includes oxygen mass. A net sink removes more from the stated reservoir than it returns during the interval. If a flux varies, account for each interval rather than multiplying one rate over the whole history. Stock S in this card is an amount, distinct from solar irradiance S in the next card.

formulas.meaning: Constant rates over the specified interval.
symbols: S: reservoir stock; F: flux in stock units per time; Δt: interval.

simple.title: A changing stock
simple.given: A reservoir gains 8 and loses 5 Gt C/year for 2 years.
steps: Net rate=8−5=3 Gt C/year.
Multiply by 2 years.
Change=+6 Gt C.

challenge.title: Convert reporting units
challenge.given: A process adds 44 tonnes CO₂ to air.
steps: One CO₂ formula unit has carbon mass fraction 12/44.
Multiply 44 by 12/44.
The addition contains 12 tonnes C.

formula_cards.watch: A large stock is not automatically a large current flux.

formula_cards.title: Climate, weather and energy balance
background: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes statistical patterns over longer periods. Local cold weather alone does not determine a global long-term trend. Compare location, timescale, uncertainty and the measured variable.

Albedo a is the reflected fraction of incoming shortwave radiation, with 0≤a≤1. For a spherical planet receiving parallel flux S, intercepted area is πr² and surface area is 4πr², giving globally averaged absorbed flux S(1−a)/4. S is in W/m²; a is dimensionless.

At steady energy balance, absorbed energy rate equals outgoing energy rate. A positive net flux stores energy; temperature response also depends on heat capacity and feedbacks. Greenhouse gases absorb/emit infrared and affect outgoing energy transfer; the effect is distinct from reflecting incoming sunlight.

A positive feedback reinforces an initial change, such as warming reducing reflective ice and increasing absorption. A negative feedback opposes change. Positive does not mean beneficial, and a feedback is different from the initial forcing.

A temperature anomaly ΔT is temperature relative to a stated baseline; a change of 1 K equals a change of 1°C. Net flux F_net is energy gain minus loss per area per time. Effective heat capacity per area C tells how much energy raises that layer by 1 K. For seconds as the time unit, C is in J/(m² K), warming rate r is K/s, and C r is W/m². A steady net flux gives ΔT = F_net Δt/C; it describes a change over time, not an equilibrium temperature.

A supplied linear climate-box model can represent F_net = F₀ − λΔT. F₀ is an imposed extra energy input at the reference state (forcing); positive λ, called lambda, is the extra restoring energy loss per kelvin, in W/(m² K). Warming increases that restoring term. The model combines this budget with heat storage: C r = F₀ − λΔT. When r = 0 there is no further storage change. If time is in years and r in K/year, use the supplied C in W year/(m² K), not a number quoted in SI heat-capacity units without conversion. Constant coefficients and the allowed temperature range are model assumptions.

formulas.meaning: A whole-sphere average for the stated geometry.
symbols: F_abs,S: W/m²; a: reflected fraction.

formulas.meaning: Heat storage equals the remaining energy imbalance in the stated linear box model.
symbols: r: warming rate; C: capacity per area with the matching time unit; F_net and F₀: W/m²; λ: W/(m² K); ΔT: K relative to the baseline.

simple.title: Absorbed average
simple.given: S=1200 W/m² and a=0.30.
steps: The absorbed fraction is 0.70.
Disk-to-sphere averaging divides by 4.

challenge.title: A feedback
challenge.given: Warming melts ice; darker exposed water absorbs more sunlight.
steps: The initial change is warming.
The resulting albedo reduction increases absorption.
That reinforces warming: positive feedback.

formula_cards.watch: An energy imbalance is a rate per area; temperature is a stored-energy response.

formula_cards.title: Deep time and the expanding universe
background: Radioactive dating infers elapsed time from a parent population when decay rate is known and the relevant system has remained closed. Initial daughter content, contamination and later loss can change the inference. Geological event order provides a separate check on radiometric ages.

A spectral redshift z=(λ_observed−λ_rest)/λ_rest is dimensionless. Known spectral lines identify the rest wavelength. A trend of larger redshift with distance supports an expanding-universe interpretation; it is one part of the evidence alongside the cosmic microwave background and light-element abundances. The model describes cosmic evolution from an early hot dense state.

For the small-redshift teaching model used here, recession speed v≈cz and v=Hd. c is light speed, H an expansion-rate parameter, and d distance. These approximations are stated when needed; they are not used for large-redshift precision.

The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is nearly all-sky thermal radiation, observed at about 2.7 K. In the hot expanding-universe model it is relic radiation released when the early universe became transparent, then stretched and cooled as space expanded. The large-scale redshift–distance trend, this background spectrum, and primordial light-element abundances are different evidence types. Hydrogen and helium formed early; stars later make many heavier elements. Agreement across these tests supports the model without observing an initial singularity or establishing every detail of cosmic history.

Here λ means wavelength, with subscripts identifying the same spectral line at rest and as observed; it is distinct from the climate restoring coefficient λ. One nm is 10⁻⁹ m. c is light speed; H is the supplied present expansion-rate parameter; d is distance. H in km/(s Mpc) gives d in megaparsecs (Mpc, a distance unit). Small-z v≈cz and v=Hd are stipulated approximations; local peculiar motions and large-redshift effects can limit a distance inference.

A radioactive parent is an unstable isotope; its daughter is the decay product. Half-life h is the time in which half a parent population decays. In the one-parent/one-retained-daughter model, initial parent count equals surviving parent plus daughters produced by this decay, after subtracting any initial daughter count. A closed system has no relevant later gain/loss. Mineral closure may occur during cooling; date only the event justified by the stated assumptions.

formulas.meaning: Compare wavelengths of the same identified line.
symbols: z: dimensionless; both λ values use the same wavelength unit.

simple.title: One line
simple.given: A known 500 nm line is observed at 510 nm.
steps: Shift=10 nm.
Divide by the rest value 500 nm.

challenge.title: Model limits
challenge.given: Two nearby galaxies follow a common v=Hd relation.
steps: A proportional speed-distance trend agrees with the stated expansion model.
One line shift alone does not measure age or prove every detail of cosmic history.
Use multiple objects, identified lines and independent evidence.
challenge.answer: An expansion interpretation, with stated limits.

formula_cards.watch: A redshift is a fractional wavelength change, not a wavelength in nm.

learning_map.big_idea: Earth and space explanations connect geometry, moving material, energy balance and records of past change. Match each inference to what the observation actually measures.

basics.title: Geometry explains changing illumination
basics.story: Earth’s rotation gives the daily cycle. Its tilted axis and orbit change solar angle and day length through the year. Moon phases describe the sunlit part visible from Earth.
basics.why: Seasons follow tilt and illumination, not a claim that summer occurs simply because Earth is closer to the Sun. An eclipse requires a particular alignment; it does not cause ordinary moon phases.

basics.title: Rocks record processes and relative order
basics.story: Plate motion, melting, cooling, erosion and deposition move or transform material. Sedimentary layers and features cutting through them preserve evidence about event order.
basics.why: Use superposition only for an appropriately interpreted sequence and allow for folding or overturning. A feature must already exist before another can cut it.

basics.title: Reservoirs change when inputs and outputs differ
basics.story: A reservoir stores material, such as carbon in the atmosphere or ocean. A flux is a transfer rate between reservoirs.
basics.why: Equal inputs and outputs keep a stock steady while material still moves. A small persistent imbalance accumulates over time.
basics.symbols: S: stock in a stated mass unit; F_in,F_out: transfer rates in that unit per time; Δt: interval. Use matching time units.

basics.title: Climate is an energy-storage problem
basics.story: Absorbed solar energy supplies input; outgoing radiation removes energy. A persistent imbalance changes energy storage and can change temperature.
basics.why: Weather is a short-term state; climate concerns the statistical pattern over longer intervals. An energy-balance model must state its area basis, feedbacks and other assumptions.

basics.title: Remote observations require an inference model
basics.story: Spectra, distances and geological clocks provide evidence about systems we cannot directly replay. Redshift compares observed spectral wavelengths with identified reference wavelengths.
basics.why: Several explanations can affect a measurement. Separate what was directly observed from the model used to infer age, motion or history.

routes.title: Explain the geometry and geological record
routes.cue: Illumination, plate motion or event order is given.
routes.connection: Draw the geometry or sequence and identify the evidence that supports each step.

routes.title: Balance matter and energy
routes.cue: A reservoir changes or a climate model receives unequal fluxes.
routes.connection: Use a common basis and matching time units; a balanced flow is different from no flow.

routes.title: Infer deep time or a remote system
routes.cue: Spectral shifts or large-scale historical evidence enters.
routes.connection: Use the supplied interpretation model and state which competing explanations are excluded.

learning_map.checkpoint: Can you separate the direct observation from its interpretation and check the geometry, reservoir boundary and time scale?

steps: Rearrange: V₂=V₁(P₁/P₂)(T₂/T₁).
worked_solution.check: Lower pressure tends to expand the gas by 1.57 while cooling contracts it by 0.833; the net factor is 1.31, so expansion is reasonable.

questions.context: A 6.0 L cylinder is divided by a frictionless sealed piston. Both gases remain at 300 K. Initially the left side is 1.5 L at 300 kPa and the right side is 4.5 L at 90 kPa.

worked_solution.model: Each side keeps its own gas and remains isothermal. At equilibrium both sides have the same pressure and their volumes sum to 6.0 L.
steps: Left side: PV_L=300×1.5=450 kPa·L, so V_L=450/P.
Right side: PV_R=90×4.5=405 kPa·L, so V_R=405/P.
Solve P=142.5 kPa.

questions.context: A vertical cylinder contains 5.0 L of gas beneath a 50 kg piston of area 0.010 m². Atmospheric pressure is 100 kPa. The gas is at 300 K and the piston moves freely. It is heated slowly to 360 K. Use g=9.8 m s⁻².

questions.feedback_incorrect: First use force balance to decide whether pressure is constant, then convert volume change to displacement.
questions.explanation: The load fixes the pressure at 149 kPa. Hence V₂/V₁=360/300, so ΔV=1.0 L. Dividing 0.001 m³ by 0.010 m² gives 0.10 m=10 cm.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Force balance on a loaded piston followed by thermal expansion
worked_solution.model: Atmospheric pressure and piston weight fix a constant external pressure; a freely moving piston matches it.
steps: Because pressure is constant, V₂=5.0×360/300=6.0 L.
worked_solution.check: A 20% temperature rise gives a 20% volume rise at constant pressure.
worked_solution.common_error: Using only atmospheric pressure or mixing litres with square metres.

questions.prompt: Estimate the bubble volume just before it reaches the surface.
questions.hint: The initial pressure includes both atmosphere and the water column; temperature is not constant.
questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The initial pressure is 100+ρgh=217.6 kPa. Thus V₂=4.0×217.6×300/(100×285)=9.16 cm³.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The initial pressure includes both atmosphere and the water column; temperature is not constant.
questions.explanation: The initial pressure is 100+ρgh=217.6 kPa. Thus V₂=4.0×217.6×300/(100×285)=9.16 cm³.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Hydrostatic pressure combined with the gas law
worked_solution.model: The bubble’s initial absolute pressure includes atmospheric pressure and water pressure; temperature also changes.
steps: Water pressure: ρgh=1000×9.8×12=117600 Pa=117.6 kPa.
Initial absolute pressure: P₁=100+117.6=217.6 kPa.
worked_solution.check: Pressure falls by more than half on rising, so the bubble should more than double in volume.
worked_solution.common_error: Using 117.6 kPa as the absolute pressure and omitting atmospheric pressure.

questions.context: A syringe is compressed rapidly and clamped. Its pressure jumps from 100 kPa to 230 kPa, then falls to 190 kPa over one minute while the measured volume stays fixed.
questions.prompt: Explain the complete pressure history using the particle model and state which reading is suitable for a Boyle-law test.
questions.hint: Link work, temperature, particle collisions and the measurement condition in one causal chain.
questions.feedback_correct: Good. The explanation links the physical model to the evidence.
questions.feedback_partial: The main idea is present, but one or more links in the reasoning chain are missing.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Link work, temperature, particle collisions and the measurement condition in one causal chain.
questions.explanation: Rapid work raises temperature and collision momentum, causing the pressure overshoot. At fixed volume the gas then transfers energy to the surroundings, particles slow and pressure falls. The settled 190 kPa reading is appropriate for an approximately isothermal Boyle-law comparison.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Thermal transient in a Boyle’s-law measurement
worked_solution.model: Rapid compression is not isothermal; the later settled reading is closer to the controlled-temperature state.
steps: Work done during rapid compression raises internal energy and temperature.
Faster particles produce the 230 kPa pressure overshoot.
While clamped, the gas loses thermal energy at fixed volume and pressure falls.
After thermal equilibrium, 190 kPa is the suitable Boyle-law reading.
worked_solution.check: A Boyle comparison requires equal temperatures; the later reading is the one taken after that condition is approximately restored.
worked_solution.common_error: Treating the immediate peak as the isothermal pressure.

questions.context: At constant temperature, the same trapped gas gives 100 kPa when the syringe scale reads 80 cm³ and 160 kPa when it reads 40 cm³. The tube and sensor contain an unrecorded volume d.

questions.explanation: Use the actual volumes: 100(80+d)=160(40+d). Solving gives d=26.7 cm³.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Finding hidden dead volume
worked_solution.model: The actual trapped volume is the syringe reading plus the same unknown dead volume d in both states.
steps: Apply Boyle’s law: 100(80+d)=160(40+d).
Therefore 1600=60d and d=26.67 cm³.
worked_solution.check: Substitution gives equal products: 100×106.67≈160×66.67≈10667 kPa·cm³.
worked_solution.common_error: Adding d to one state only or assigning it a negative sign.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Finding a constant pressure offset
worked_solution.model: True absolute pressure equals the displayed value plus the same offset b at every reading.
steps: Set the Boyle products equal: (90+b)100=(190+b)50.
Thus 50b=500 and b=10.0 kPa.
worked_solution.check: Corrected pressures are 100 and 200 kPa while volumes are 100 and 50 cm³, giving equal PV.
worked_solution.common_error: Applying the offset to only one pressure reading.

steps: Total nR=2.0 kPa·L·K⁻¹.
worked_solution.check: The result lies between the initial pressures and uses both gas amounts rather than an unweighted average.

questions.context: Repeated compression data drift downward. The apparatus might be warming temporarily, leaking slowly or suffering a sensor offset.
questions.prompt: Design a measurement sequence that separates the three causes and state the diagnostic pattern for each.
questions.hint: Use time dependence, repeatability and an independent calibration standard.
questions.feedback_correct: Good. The explanation links the physical model to the evidence.
questions.feedback_partial: The main idea is present, but one or more links in the reasoning chain are missing.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Use time dependence, repeatability and an independent calibration standard.
questions.explanation: Wait at each volume and monitor temperature to expose thermal transients; return repeatedly to the same reference volume to reveal irreversible gas loss; check the sensor at a known pressure to identify a fixed offset. Heating decays with time, leakage produces progressive non-recovery and an offset remains reproducible.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Separating thermal drift, leakage and sensor offset
worked_solution.model: Use time behaviour, return-to-reference cycles and independent calibration because the three faults leave different signatures.
steps: At each volume, record pressure and temperature versus time; a thermal transient decays as equilibrium returns.
Cycle repeatedly back to the same reference volume; leakage causes progressive failure to recover the original settled pressure.
Check the sensor against known atmospheric pressure or another calibrated standard; a zero offset remains reproducible.
Repeat the sequence to distinguish random scatter from systematic patterns.
worked_solution.final_answer: Heating decays with time; leakage accumulates between cycles; offset is constant against a standard.
worked_solution.check: The design creates an independent observation for each proposed cause.
worked_solution.common_error: Changing several conditions at once and then assigning all drift to leakage.

questions.context: A flexible balloon is taken to an altitude where external pressure is much lower. A calculation using ideal-gas behaviour predicts a volume larger than the balloon can physically contain.
options: The gas law must be numerically wrong.
The balloon must reach the calculated volume because equations override material limits.
The ideal-gas calculation identifies the tendency, but the balloon may become taut, leak or burst so the constant-external-pressure model then fails.
The temperature must become 0 K.
questions.hint: Distinguish a mathematical result inside a model from the behaviour of the real apparatus.
questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The calculation is conditional on a freely flexible, sealed balloon. Material tension or failure introduces a new constraint.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Distinguish a mathematical result inside a model from the behaviour of the real apparatus.
questions.explanation: The calculation is conditional on a freely flexible, sealed balloon. Material tension or failure introduces a new constraint.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Recognising when an apparatus constraint invalidates a gas model
worked_solution.model: The gas-law calculation is conditional on a sealed, freely flexible balloon with negligible membrane tension.
steps: Lower external pressure predicts expansion while the balloon remains flexible.
Once the material becomes taut, membrane tension adds to the external pressure.
If stress exceeds the material limit, the balloon can leak or burst and n is no longer fixed.
The calculation still gives the initial tendency but cannot override the new physical constraint.
worked_solution.check: This conclusion identifies both the useful prediction and the condition at which the model stops applying.
worked_solution.common_error: Assuming a mathematical extrapolation guarantees that the apparatus can realise the predicted state.

questions.context: A sealed rigid container holds A₂ gas. At constant temperature, a fraction x of the molecules dissociates according to A₂→2A. The final pressure is 1.30 times the initial pressure.
questions.hint: Count gas particles before and after dissociation; mass conservation does not mean particle-number conservation.
questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Each dissociated molecule adds one extra particle, so particle number and pressure increase by the factor 1+x. Thus 1+x=1.30 and x=30%.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Count gas particles before and after dissociation; mass conservation does not mean particle-number conservation.
questions.explanation: Each dissociated molecule adds one extra particle, so particle number and pressure increase by the factor 1+x. Thus 1+x=1.30 and x=30%.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Particle-number change during dissociation
worked_solution.model: At fixed V and T, pressure is proportional to the total number of gas particles.
steps: Start with N molecules of A₂.
If fraction x dissociates, (1−x)N A₂ molecules remain and 2xN A atoms form.
Total particles=(1−x+2x)N=(1+x)N.
Therefore P_f/P_i=1+x=1.30, so x=0.30.
worked_solution.check: Complete dissociation would double pressure; partial dissociation giving a 30% rise is physically consistent.
worked_solution.common_error: Assuming mass conservation means the number of gas particles is unchanged.

Right: PV_R=100×6.0=600 kPa·L, so V_R=600/P.
Geometry gives V_L+V_R=8.0, hence 1400/P=8.0.

questions.context: Gas beneath a frictionless piston has V₁=2.0 L, P₁=100 kPa and T₁=300 K. A relaxed spring begins to compress as the piston rises. The piston area is 0.010 m² and spring constant is 500 N m⁻¹. When displacement is x metres, V=2.0+10x litres and P=100+50x kPa. The gas is heated to 450 K.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The final state obeys (100+50x)(2+10x)=100×2×450/300=300 kPa L. The positive root of 500x²+1100x−100=0 is x=0.0874 m.

worked_solution.model: The spring makes both pressure and volume depend on displacement, so substitute the supplied mechanics relations into the gas invariant.
steps: Fixed n gives P₂V₂/T₂=P₁V₁/T₁.
The roots are approximately 0.0874 m and −2.287 m; only the positive upward displacement is physical.

worked_solution.model: Every state must share the same corrected product (P_read+b)(V_read+d). Three states determine and then validate d and b.

All three agree, so the two calibration corrections are consistent.

questions.context: A rigid 2.0 L vessel contains gas at 100 kPa and 300 K. It is heated to 450 K, then a valve is opened until its pressure is 120 kPa while temperature remains 450 K. The valve is closed and the gas cools to 300 K.
questions.prompt: What percentage of the original particles escaped?
questions.hint: Compare states immediately before and after venting, where V and T are the same.
questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Before venting the pressure would be 150 kPa. At the same V and T, particle amount is proportional to pressure, so 120/150=0.80 remains and 20% escaped. Cooling afterwards changes pressure but not the escaped fraction.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Compare states immediately before and after venting, where V and T are the same.
questions.explanation: Before venting the pressure would be 150 kPa. At the same V and T, particle amount is proportional to pressure, so 120/150=0.80 remains and 20% escaped. Cooling afterwards changes pressure but not the escaped fraction.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Separating heating, venting and cooling
worked_solution.model: At fixed V, pressure tracks nT. Compare particle amount immediately before and after venting because temperature is the same then.
steps: Before venting, heating at fixed V gives P_hot=100×450/300=150 kPa.
During venting, V and T remain fixed, so n_after/n_before=P_after/P_before=120/150=0.80.
Therefore 80% remains and 20% escapes.
Later cooling changes pressure but cannot change the already closed particle amount.
worked_solution.check: The answer lies between 0% and 100%, and the pressure during venting falls by exactly 20% at fixed V and T.
worked_solution.common_error: Using the final cooled pressure to calculate the escaped fraction.

aV₀²/[R(V₀−b)]

questions.feedback_incorrect: Set pressure to its lowest physical value only after substituting the fixed volume.

At the limiting physical pressure p=0: (a/V₀²)(V₀−b)=RT_min.
Therefore T_min=a(V₀−b)/(RV₀²).
worked_solution.check: V₀>b makes the expression positive, as an absolute temperature must be.
worked_solution.common_error: Setting T=0 first or allowing negative absolute pressure.

questions.context: A vertical tube, sealed at the top and open below, is 0.50 m long. At the surface it traps air at 100 kPa filling the tube. Final pressure is 100+9.8(2.0+L) kPa and final gas length is L.
Solve [100+9.8(2+L)]L=50; the physical root is L=0.4046 m.
worked_solution.check: The final air length is positive and shorter than 0.50 m, while increased pressure is consistent with compression.

questions.context: For many settled readings, a plot of displayed pressure P_read against 1/V is nearly straight but has a positive vertical intercept. Replacing V by V+d removes curvature but the positive intercept remains.
options: Only a gas leak is present.
Dead volume explains the curvature and a pressure zero offset explains the remaining intercept.
The gas has negative absolute temperature.
Boyle's law requires plotting P against V.
questions.hint: Link each error to the feature it changes in the linearised graph.
questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Dead volume changes the horizontal variable and can create curvature; a constant pressure offset appears as a vertical intercept.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Link each error to the feature it changes in the linearised graph.
questions.explanation: Dead volume changes the horizontal variable and can create curvature; a constant pressure offset appears as a vertical intercept.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Diagnosing errors from a linearised Boyle plot
worked_solution.model: Different systematic errors change different graph features: dead volume changes the horizontal variable; pressure offset shifts the vertical reading.
steps: Curvature with V_read indicates that the actual volume is not simply V_read.
Replacing V by V+d removes curvature, supporting a fixed dead-volume correction.
A remaining positive vertical intercept means displayed pressure contains an approximately constant zero offset.
worked_solution.check: The interpretation assigns one observed graph feature to each independently meaningful apparatus error.
worked_solution.common_error: Calling the intercept a leak; leakage usually produces time-dependent non-recovery rather than a fixed vertical shift.

questions.context: You must decide whether a gas thermometer remains a reliable linear thermometer from room temperature towards very low temperature.
questions.prompt: Design the graph, controls and checks, and explain why a long extrapolation to absolute zero may fail.
questions.hint: A complete design needs a graph, controlled variables, calibration and explicit model-failure reasons.
questions.feedback_correct: Good. The explanation links the physical model to the evidence.
questions.feedback_partial: The main idea is present, but one or more links in the reasoning chain are missing.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A complete design needs a graph, controlled variables, calibration and explicit model-failure reasons.
questions.explanation: Use a rigid sealed bulb, calibrated absolute-pressure sensor and independent temperature standard; wait for equilibrium and plot P against Celsius temperature. A linear fit can estimate the zero-pressure intercept, but sensor offset, leaks, non-equilibrium, real-gas effects, condensation and the long extrapolation limit confidence.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Testing and extrapolating a constant-volume gas thermometer
worked_solution.model: For fixed n and V, ideal-gas pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature, so P versus Celsius temperature should be linear over the valid range.
steps: Use a rigid sealed bulb, calibrated absolute-pressure sensor and independent calibrated temperature standard.
Wait for thermal equilibrium at many temperatures and repeat readings while checking for leaks.
Plot P against Celsius temperature; use gradient, intercept, uncertainty and residuals.
A zero-pressure extrapolation estimates absolute zero, but it is far outside the measured range.
At low temperature real-gas forces, condensation, sensor offset and non-equilibrium can invalidate the linear model.
worked_solution.final_answer: Use the fit only over the tested domain; treat the absolute-zero intercept as an uncertain extrapolation.
worked_solution.check: Residuals and repeat runs can reveal systematic failure before trusting a long extrapolation.
worked_solution.common_error: Claiming that a straight section near room temperature proves linearity down to 0 K.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Limits of the ideal-gas model
worked_solution.model: The ideal model neglects intermolecular forces and particle volume. Dense, cool gas makes these assumptions weak.
steps: Near condensation, particles are close enough for attractive forces to matter.
Attraction pulls particles back from the wall and reduces momentum transfer relative to the ideal prediction.
Finite molecular volume can also matter at high density, but the observed lower pressure is especially consistent with attraction.
worked_solution.check: The explanation predicts the stated direction: measured pressure below the ideal value.

The readings require a negative dead volume, so offset plus dead volume is not a physically adequate error model.
The gas temperature must be exactly 0 K.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Solving the three-state equations gives d=−8 cm³ and b=−18 kPa. A negative unrecorded volume is unphysical, so an additional effect such as leakage, temperature drift or scale error must be investigated.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Solve for the two calibration parameters, then judge whether their signs and sizes are physically possible.
questions.explanation: Solving the three-state equations gives d=−8 cm³ and b=−18 kPa. A negative unrecorded volume is unphysical, so an additional effect such as leakage, temperature drift or scale error must be investigated.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Testing whether a calibration model is physically admissible
worked_solution.model: Solve the common-product model for d and b, then judge whether the fitted parameters can represent the apparatus.
steps: Solving the independent equalities gives d=−8 cm³ and b=−18 kPa.
A dead volume represents extra trapped space and cannot be negative.
Therefore offset plus dead volume cannot explain all three readings; investigate temperature drift, leakage or scale nonlinearity.
worked_solution.check: A numerical fit is not sufficient when a fitted physical parameter has an impossible sign.
worked_solution.common_error: Accepting every algebraic parameter without checking its physical meaning.

questions.context: A student claims that a good fit to PV=constant proves that air is an ideal gas under all conditions.

questions.hint: Separate evidence for a model within a tested domain from proof under every possible condition.

worked_solution.tested_idea: Evaluating evidence and designing a model-failure test
worked_solution.model: A fit supports a model only for the tested range and after apparatus errors have been checked.
steps: Use calibrated absolute pressure and actual total gas volume, including dead volume.
Hold temperature constant, wait for equilibrium and repeat compression/expansion cycles to check leaks and hysteresis.
Test a wide range of pressures and several temperatures, especially high density and low temperature.

concept_discussion.given: A transparent block appears to have a refractive index that increases with incidence angle. The data came from one hand-drawn normal and white light.
concept_discussion.prompt: Decide whether this is convincing evidence of a variable refractive index and design a stronger test.

application_brief.title: Gas thermometers and phase change
application_brief.background: A gas thermometer infers temperature from gas pressure in a sealed bulb. At sufficiently low temperature a real gas can form liquid: condensation transfers particles out of the gas phase. In liquid–vapour equilibrium, evaporation and condensation balance on average. concept_discussion.given: A volatile liquid on a thermometer cools below room temperature. Strong airflow makes the minimum temperature lower.

questions.feedback_incorrect: A slower initial temperature rise does not establish a universal steady insulation advantage.
questions.explanation: During the first two minutes, input can increase panel internal energy as well as pass through the panel. A lower inner-face temperature could arise from greater energy storage, greater resistance or both; the unknown capacities allow competing explanations. Choose Option 3. concept_discussion.given: Two explanations fit a gas-volume plateau: reactant X is exhausted, or the reaction is reversible and reaches equilibrium.
concept_discussion.prompt: Design a test that distinguishes them.
concept_discussion.discussion_points: Adding X alone can restart production both when X was exhausted and when a reversible reaction was at equilibrium, so it is not a decisive test. Detectable X rules out complete X exhaustion but does not by itself prove equilibrium; where an equilibrium law is supplied, test the reaction quotient and compare responses to controlled perturbations. Check mixing and possible surface inhibition as alternative causes.

questions.given: A bottom mark is viewed through a liquid of unknown depth d and a 0.0400 m glass cover of index 1.60. The cover touches the liquid; there is no air gap. Its near-normal apparent depth below the cover top is 0.2250 m. In a separate oblique-ray measurement, a ray from the same mark reaches the liquid/glass boundary 0.1500 m horizontally from its vertical line; its angle inside the glass is 25.0° to the normal. All interfaces are parallel. Air index is 1.00.

questions.explanation: Let n be the liquid refractive index and i its ray angle to the normal. In the near-normal observation, each layer contributes thickness/index: 0.2250=d/n+0.0400/1.60, so d/n=0.2000 m and d=(0.2000 m)n. In the separate oblique observation, the ray travels 0.1500 m horizontally while rising d. The right triangle gives sin i=0.1500/√(d²+0.1500²), with both lengths in m. Snell’s law at the liquid/glass boundary gives n sin i=1.60sin25.0°. Write k=1.60sin25.0°=0.676189 (dimensionless). Substitute d=0.2000n using m for lengths: 0.1500n/√(0.0400n²+0.02250)=k. Square and collect terms: 0.02250n²=k²(0.0400n²+0.02250), so n²=0.02250k²/(0.02250−0.0400k²)=2.44322. Select the positive physical index n=1.56308. Then d=0.312616 m. The liquid angle is arctan(0.1500/0.312616)=25.633°; the given glass angle is 25.0°. The near-normal approximation applies to the depth observation, not to this oblique ray.

questions.given: A parallel plate has front reflectance R_f, back reflectance R_b and an unknown one-pass internal intensity factor a, with 0<a≤1. Later reflected paths are excluded from these signals; ignore interference.
questions.context: A parallel plate has front reflectance R_f, back reflectance R_b and an unknown one-pass internal intensity factor a, with 0<a≤1. At a surface, the nonreflected fraction 1−R is transmitted. A narrow beam gives separated first-path signals: front reflection 0.100 I₀, first back reflection 0.0810 I₀ and first forward transmitted beam 0.648 I₀. Later reflected paths are excluded from these signals; ignore interference.
questions.hint: Count each path’s surface crossings and interior traversals before eliminating unknowns.
questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Both measured outgoing paths are reproduced with 0<a<1 and 0<R_b<1; the other quadratic root is negative.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Assuming equal surfaces or ignoring internal loss removes an unknown without evidence.
questions.explanation: Front reflection gives R_f=0.100. The first back image crosses the front twice and the interior twice:0.9²a²R_b=0.0810, hence a²R_b=0.100. questions.context: A student predicts that a rolling sphere and a sliding frictionless block released from the same height must arrive together because both lose the same gravitational potential energy. The sphere arrives later. Both start from rest on straight inclines of equal angle and length; the sphere rolls without slipping and air resistance is negligible.
questions.prompt: Explain why the equal-energy argument does not imply equal final speeds or equal travel times.
questions.hint: Separate translational energy from rotational energy and compare accelerations.
questions.feedback_correct: Correct. For a solid sphere a=5g sinθ/7, below the slider’s g sinθ.
questions.feedback_partial: Partly correct. State both the governing principle and how the constraint changes the result.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Energy equality alone does not state how energy is partitioned or determine equal travel times.
questions.explanation: Both lose mgh per unit mass for the same vertical drop, but the sphere stores part as rotational kinetic energy. For a solid sphere I=2mR²/5 and ω=v/R, so mgh=½mv²+½Iω²=7mv²/10. Its final v²=10gh/7; the slider has v²=2gh. For equal straight inclines, translation and torque give sphere acceleration a=5g sinθ/7, while the frictionless slider has a=g sinθ. Both start from rest and cover the same distance, so t=√(2s/a); the sphere takes √(7/5) times as long. A matched release controls height, angle, path length and start time; check rolling without slip and compare travel times within timing uncertainty.
